Bowed, plucked and full of possibilities.

StringsMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Violin

A little wooden box with a great big voice

In a few notes

  • Section: Strings.
  • How it sounds: Four strings, usually bowed; bright, singing and sometimes wonderfully scratchy.
  • When it began: The violin family took shape in northern Italy in the early 1500s. Andrea Amati was an important early maker.
  • Players to know: Niccolò Paganini, Itzhak Perlman, Hilary Hahn and Nicola Benedetti.
  • A surprise: First and second violins are the same instrument: they play different musical parts.

The story

Imagine a tiny wooden boat tucked under someone’s chin. It has curved sides, two holes shaped like the letter f, and four strings stretched along its front. This is a violin. Its wooden body helps a small vibration become a sound that can travel across a concert hall.

The player draws a bow across the strings. The bow’s hair is usually horsehair, made slightly sticky with a substance called rosin. It catches and releases the string very quickly. The left hand presses a string against the fingerboard to change its vibrating length. Shorter lengths make higher notes. Plucking a string with a finger is called pizzicato.

Violin makers in northern Italy developed the familiar instrument in the early 1500s. Andrea Amati and, later, Antonio Stradivari became famous for their careful work. There was no single morning when every violin suddenly became modern: makers changed the design over many years.

In an orchestra, violins often sit near the front in two teams. They can carry a melody, shimmer quietly behind another instrument, or race through a storm of notes. A fiddle in a folk band is also a violin! Listen for the moment one violin steps forward from the group. Does its tune sound like a voice telling you a story?

StringsMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Viola

The warm voice in the middle

In a few notes

  • Section: Strings.
  • How it sounds: Four bowed strings, tuned lower than a violin; warm and mellow.
  • When it began: Violas developed alongside violins in Italy during the 1500s; their sizes and shapes continued to vary.
  • Players to know: Lionel Tertis, William Primrose, Tabea Zimmermann and Timothy Ridout.
  • A surprise: The viola’s lowest string is C; a violin’s lowest string is G.

The story

At first you might mistake a viola for a violin. Look again: it is usually a little larger. Listen again: its voice reaches lower and often sounds darker and warmer. The viola belongs to the string family and helps fill the musical space between the violin and the cello.

A viola player holds the instrument under the chin and moves a bow across four strings. The strings are tuned C, G, D and A, from low to high. Three of those notes match the violin’s strings, but the viola has a low C instead of a high E. That small change gives it a different musical personality.

The viola and violin developed together in northern Italy in the 1500s. Makers tried instruments of different sizes. Even today, violas are not all exactly the same length. A maker must balance a lovely low sound with a size the musician can comfortably hold and play.

In an orchestra, violas often weave important patterns inside the music. You may not notice them straight away, but take them away and something would be missing. They also make wonderful solo instruments. Listen to a viola melody and imagine a person speaking in a calm, thoughtful voice. Then hear a lively passage: the warm middle voice can dance and sparkle too.

StringsMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Cello

A singing voice you can hug

In a few notes

  • Section: Strings.
  • How it sounds: Four bowed strings; rich low notes and a singing upper voice.
  • When it began: Cellos developed in Italy in the 1500s. Their familiar size became more settled around 1700.
  • Players to know: Pablo Casals, Jacqueline du Pré, Yo-Yo Ma and Sheku Kanneh-Mason.
  • A surprise: An endpin rests on the floor and helps support the cello.

The story

A cello is too large to fit under anyone’s chin. Its player sits on a chair and holds it between the knees, with a metal spike called an endpin resting on the floor. The instrument’s full name is violoncello, but most people use the shorter name. Say it “chell-oh”.

Like a violin, the cello has four strings and a hollow wooden body. A bow sets its strings vibrating, and fingers pressing on the fingerboard choose the notes. Its long strings can make deep sounds, but the player can also travel high up the fingerboard. That gives the cello a surprisingly wide musical voice.

The cello developed in Italy during the 1500s as part of the violin family. Early examples came in different sizes. Around 1700, makers including Antonio Stradivari helped establish sizes closer to the cellos we recognise today. Changes to strings, bows and playing techniques continued afterwards.

In the orchestra, cellos can support the other strings with low notes or sing a melody of their own. Sometimes they pluck a bouncy rhythm instead of using their bows. A cello can sound gentle, fierce, playful or very still. When you listen, notice where the player’s bow changes direction. Can a whole musical sentence seem to flow even though the bow must keep moving back and forth?

Double bass

The gentle giant of the strings

In a few notes

  • Section: Strings.
  • How it sounds: Usually four long strings; very low bowed or plucked notes.
  • When it began: The double bass grew from several European bowed-bass traditions during the 1500s and 1600s; it has no single known inventor.
  • Players to know: Domenico Dragonetti, Giovanni Bottesini, Gary Karr and jazz musician Esperanza Spalding.
  • A surprise: Most double-bass music sounds an octave lower than the notes written on the page.

The story

Meet the tallest regular member of the orchestra’s string family. A double bass can stand taller than its player! Musicians usually stand beside it or sit on a high stool. Its long strings and roomy wooden body help it make the low notes that give an orchestra a strong foundation.

Players can bow the strings for long, flowing sounds or pluck them for short, springy ones. They use one of two main kinds of bow hold. Unlike the violin, viola and cello, a usual four-string double bass is tuned in fourths: E, A, D and G. Some orchestral basses have an extra string or a special extension to reach still lower.

The double bass did not appear through one person’s invention. It grew from different European bowed-bass instruments during the 1500s and 1600s. That mixed history helps explain why modern basses can have slightly different shoulder shapes and body outlines.

Listen to the basses in an orchestra as if you were following a giant’s footsteps. Their notes may move slowly beneath a busy tune, then suddenly leap into quick action. In jazz, a plucked bass often supplies a walking pattern that keeps the music moving. Famous bass players have also shown that this giant can be a nimble solo storyteller, not simply the lowest voice in the room.

Harp

A rainbow of plucked strings

In a few notes

  • Section: Strings.
  • How it sounds: Plucked strings; rippling, ringing notes.
  • When it began: Harps existed in ancient cultures more than 4,000 years ago. Sébastien Érard patented the double-action pedal harp in 1810.
  • Players to know: Marcel Grandjany, Nicanor Zabaleta, Marisa Robles and Catrin Finch.
  • A surprise: A full-size concert harp usually has 47 strings and seven pedals.

The story

A concert harp looks like a tall wooden triangle filled with strings. Its player leans it gently towards one shoulder and plucks with the fingers of both hands. Long strings make lower sounds and short strings make higher ones. The large wooden soundboard helps those vibrations reach our ears.

Harps have a very long story. Pictures and surviving instruments show that people played them in ancient cultures more than four thousand years ago. Those instruments did not all look like today’s concert harp. There was no single inventor of the whole harp family: many communities developed their own designs.

The modern orchestral harp has an extra puzzle beneath it: seven pedals. Each pedal changes all the strings with one letter name, such as all the C strings. Sébastien Érard patented an important double-action pedal system in 1810. It lets a player raise each string’s note in two steps, making many more musical keys possible.

Harpists can play separate notes, rich groups of notes called chords, and sweeping glissandos. For a glissando, a finger brushes across a row of strings, making a sparkling slide. But harp music is not always dreamy. It can be sharp, rhythmic and powerful. Watch both hands and both feet during a performance: making that floating sound can involve a remarkable amount of careful movement.

The Bible mentions ancient harps and lyres, including in Psalm 150. Those plucked instruments were much smaller and simpler than today’s orchestral pedal harp. David’s kinnor is often understood as a lyre, although some translations call it a harp.

Guitar

Six plucked strings and a wooden singing box

In a few notes

  • Section: Strings · An occasional orchestral guest.
  • How it sounds: Usually six nylon or nylon-cored strings, plucked with fingers; intimate and clear.
  • When it began: The modern six-string classical guitar developed around 1800. Spanish maker Antonio de Torres shaped its familiar larger design during the mid-1800s.
  • Players to know: Andrés Segovia, Julian Bream, John Williams, Berta Rojas and Xuefei Yang.
  • A surprise: A guitarist can play a melody and its bass accompaniment at the same time.

The story

A classical guitar is an acoustic instrument: its hollow wooden body helps the strings speak without needing a loudspeaker. The player usually plucks with the right-hand fingers while the left hand presses strings against metal strips called frets. A fret helps choose the length of string that vibrates.

Most classical guitars have six strings. Modern strings use nylon and related materials; the lower strings usually have metal wound around a flexible core. Earlier players used gut strings. The thumb often plays low notes while other fingers pick out a higher tune. One musician can sound like a tiny ensemble.

Guitars have a long history, and older instruments came with different numbers of strings and string pairs. The familiar six-string form developed around 1800. During the mid-1800s, the Spanish maker Antonio de Torres helped shape the larger body and internal bracing that influenced modern classical guitars.

The guitar is an orchestral guest, not a regular member of the symphonic string section. Its gentle sound needs space around it, especially in a concerto. Rodrigo’s Concierto de Aranjuez gives the guitar wonderful conversations with the orchestra. Listen for plucked bass notes, ringing chords and a tune above them. How does the player keep one musical voice singing while another moves underneath?

WoodwindMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Flute

Air that turns into birdsong

In a few notes

  • Section: Woodwind.
  • How it sounds: Air blown across an opening; clear, bright and breathy.
  • When it began: Flutes are prehistoric. Theobald Boehm developed a key design close to the modern concert flute in 1847.
  • Players to know: Jean-Pierre Rampal, James Galway, Emmanuel Pahud and Jasmine Choi.
  • A surprise: A metal concert flute belongs to the woodwind family even though it has no reed.

The story

The flute player holds a shiny tube sideways and blows across a small opening near one end. The air stream meets an edge, rather like blowing across the top of a bottle. Inside the tube, air begins vibrating. That moving air makes the flute’s clear, light voice.

The player presses keys that open and close holes along the tube. Changing the open holes changes the vibrating air column and helps choose the notes. Breath, lips and tongue matter too. A player can make a smooth flowing line or separate little notes that seem to hop like birds on a branch.

Flutes are among the oldest known musical instruments. Prehistoric bone flutes are tens of thousands of years old. The modern orchestral flute has a much newer design. In 1847, the German maker and player Theobald Boehm developed an important system of holes and keys that still shapes concert flutes today.

Most concert flutes are metal, but they remain in the woodwind family. Musical families are about history and how sounds are made, not simply what an instrument is built from. In the orchestra, flutes can sparkle high above the strings or play gentle, breathy melodies. Listen for a quick flutter of notes, then a long floating phrase. How does the player make enough space to breathe?

The Bible mentions pipes or flutes, including in Psalm 150, depending on the translation. These were ancient wind instruments, not the modern keyed metal concert flute. Some ancient instrument words have uncertain meanings.

WoodwindMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Piccolo

Small instrument, sky-high sound

In a few notes

  • Section: Woodwind.
  • How it sounds: A small flute sounding an octave above the concert flute.
  • When it began: The modern orchestral piccolo developed from earlier small flutes, becoming established during the 1700s; later makers added improved key systems.
  • Players to know: Jean-Louis Beaumadier, Nicola Mazzanti and orchestral piccolo specialist Jan Gippo.
  • A surprise: Piccolo means “small” in Italian, but its sound can carry over a whole orchestra.

The story

If the flute is a bird, the piccolo might be a tiny bird with an astonishingly strong call. It is roughly half the length of a concert flute. A player holds it sideways and blows across its mouth hole. Its short tube helps it reach some of the highest notes in the orchestra.

The piccolo is a woodwind instrument, even when parts of it are made from metal. Many orchestral piccolos have wooden bodies. Its fingerings are similar to the flute’s, but controlling such a small air stream takes care. A very small movement of the lips can make a noticeable difference to the sound.

Small flutes have existed for centuries. The orchestral piccolo became established during the 1700s, and makers later added more useful keys. It has no single agreed inventor. As with many instruments, the familiar design grew through the work of many players and makers.

Piccolo music is written so that it sounds an octave higher than the notes on the page. That means the same named note rings out in a higher register. Composers use it for sparkling dances, birdsong and exciting climaxes. It can also sound surprisingly soft. Listen to a march with a piccolo solo and notice how its little tune can fly above much larger instruments. Tiny does not mean timid!

WoodwindMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Oboe

Two tiny reeds, one clear voice

In a few notes

  • Section: Woodwind.
  • How it sounds: Two reeds vibrating together; clear, focused and sometimes plaintive.
  • When it began: The modern oboe developed in France in the mid-1600s from the louder shawm; the Hotteterre family helped shape it.
  • Players to know: Léon Goossens, Heinz Holliger, Albrecht Mayer and Nicholas Daniel.
  • A surprise: Before many concerts, the oboe gives an A so the orchestra can tune together.

The story

An oboe looks like a slim wooden tube covered in silver keys. At the top is something very small and very important: a double reed. It is made from two thin pieces of cane tied together. When the player blows, those pieces vibrate against each other and start the sound.

The oboist’s fingers operate keys that open and close holes. The breath must be carefully controlled through the tiny opening in the reed. Players often make or adjust their own reeds, trimming them with great patience. A small change to a reed can change how the whole instrument feels and sounds.

The oboe developed in France during the middle of the 1600s. Makers, including members of the Hotteterre family, helped turn the outdoor shawm into an instrument suited to more delicate music. Later generations added keys and changed the design further. It was a long development rather than a single finished invention.

In an orchestra, the oboe can sound like a clear voice calling across a landscape. It often plays tender solos, but it can be lively and funny too. Before a concert, an oboist usually sounds an A for the other players to match. Listen for the oboe’s focused tone, then notice how differently a flute makes its sound. Both use breath, but their musical colours are wonderfully different.

WoodwindMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Cor anglais

The oboe’s thoughtful cousin

In a few notes

  • Section: Woodwind.
  • How it sounds: Double reed; lower and mellower than an oboe.
  • When it began: The cor anglais developed in Europe in the early 1700s; its straight modern form and keywork evolved later.
  • Players to know: Louis Rosenblatt, Thomas Stacy and Christine Pendrill.
  • A surprise: Its name means “English horn”, but it is an oboe-family woodwind, not a brass horn.

The story

Here is an instrument with a puzzling name. Cor anglais means “English horn” in French, but the instrument is not a brass horn. It belongs to the oboe family. You may also hear people call it the English horn. Its voice is lower than the oboe’s and often sounds warm, distant or thoughtful.

Look for its pear-shaped bell and the small bent metal tube near the top. That tube holds a double reed, made from two pieces of cane. The player blows through the reed and presses keys along the wooden body. Like an oboe, it needs careful breath and very precise finger movements.

The cor anglais developed in Europe in the early 1700s. Early instruments could be curved or angled. Later makers developed a straight body and more elaborate keys. Its name has a complicated history, and no single person can confidently be named as its inventor.

Orchestras do not need a cor anglais for every piece. Often an oboist changes instruments when the score asks for it. When it appears, it may have a particularly memorable melody. Dvořák gave it the famous slow tune in his New World Symphony. Listen as if a storyteller were speaking slowly beside you. Notice the spaces between phrases: sometimes a musical breath is just as important as the notes themselves.

WoodwindMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Clarinet

A voice with many colours

In a few notes

  • Section: Woodwind.
  • How it sounds: One cane reed against a mouthpiece; woody low notes and bright high notes.
  • When it began: Johann Christoph Denner is generally credited with developing the clarinet around 1700 in Nuremberg; later makers greatly expanded its keys.
  • Players to know: Benny Goodman, Sabine Meyer, Martin Fröst and Emma Johnson.
  • A surprise: The opening of Gershwin’s Rhapsody in Blue makes a clarinet swoop upwards.

The story

A clarinet can whisper in a low, woody voice and then jump into a bright, ringing one. Its sound begins with a single thin reed fixed against a mouthpiece. The player’s breath makes the reed vibrate. That vibration sets the air inside the instrument moving.

Most orchestral clarinets have dark wooden bodies, though other materials are used too. Fingers cover some holes directly and press keys to reach others. The player’s tongue can separate notes, while steady breath helps join them into a smooth line. A special register key helps the clarinet leap into its higher voice.

Around 1700, the German maker Johann Christoph Denner developed the clarinet from an earlier single-reed instrument called the chalumeau. He is generally credited with its invention, although details of the earliest changes are uncertain. Makers and players added many more keys in the centuries that followed.

Composers love the clarinet’s large range and changing colours. Mozart wrote a famous concerto for it, while jazz players found new ways to bend, swing and sparkle. The opening of Gershwin’s Rhapsody in Blue slides upwards in a wonderful musical stretch. Try listening first for the clarinet’s low sound, then its high sound. Do they feel like the same storyteller changing mood, or two characters having a conversation?

A smaller cousin: the E-flat clarinet

The E-flat clarinet is shorter and sounds higher than the usual B-flat clarinet. It still uses one reed. Small clarinets developed during the 1800s, and composers including Berlioz, Mahler and Ravel used their bright, piercing colour. In Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique, it gives a familiar tune a strange new character. Players often specialise in several clarinet sizes.

WoodwindMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Bass clarinet

A low voice with a silver smile

In a few notes

  • Section: Woodwind.
  • How it sounds: Single reed; deep, dark notes and a surprisingly agile upper voice.
  • When it began: Bass clarinets appeared in the late 1700s. Adolphe Sax made influential improvements in the 1830s.
  • Players to know: Harry Sparnaay, Eric Dolphy and Michael Lowenstern.
  • A surprise: Its curved metal bell makes it look a little like a saxophone, but most of its body is wood.

The story

Look at that long dark instrument with a curved silver bell. Is it a saxophone? No: it is a bass clarinet, a larger, lower member of the clarinet family. Its body is usually made from wood. A bent neck near the top brings the mouthpiece within comfortable reach of the player.

Like the smaller clarinet, it uses one cane reed against a mouthpiece. Its long air column helps it make deep notes. Many instruments rest on a small floor peg, so the musician does not have to carry all their weight. Some bass clarinets have extra keys and longer tubing to reach even lower.

Early bass clarinets appeared in the late 1700s in several unusual shapes. During the 1830s, the Belgian maker Adolphe Sax made influential improvements to their design. He also invented the saxophone, which helps explain why his name appears in the stories of two different woodwinds.

In orchestral music, a bass clarinet can add a dark shadow beneath other instruments or step forward with a lonely solo. It can also play quick, nimble patterns. Jazz and newer concert music give it exciting adventures of its own. Listen to its lowest notes, then wait for it to climb. Can the same voice seem like a giant one moment and a quiet, curious creature the next?

WoodwindMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Bassoon

A folded tube with a storyteller’s voice

In a few notes

  • Section: Woodwind.
  • How it sounds: Double reed; woody low sounds and expressive higher notes.
  • When it began: The jointed bassoon developed from earlier double-reed bass instruments in the 1600s. Almenräder and Heckel improved the German design during the 1800s.
  • Players to know: Milan Turković, Klaus Thunemann, Judith LeClair and Sergio Azzolini.
  • A surprise: Its long air passage doubles back inside the instrument, rather than stretching straight down to the floor.

The story

A bassoon looks rather like a bundle of long wooden pipes. Its air passage travels down one side, turns at the bottom and comes back up the other. Folding the tube this way helps put a very long instrument within a player’s reach. A curved metal tube called a bocal holds the double reed.

The player blows through two thin pieces of cane. Their vibration starts the bassoon’s sound. Both hands work many keys, and the thumbs have unusually busy jobs. Although its voice often lives low in the orchestra, the bassoon can climb into a beautifully expressive upper register.

The bassoon developed during the 1600s from earlier double-reed bass instruments, including the dulcian. Its body came to be made in separate joints. In the 1800s, Carl Almenräder and the Heckel workshop helped improve the German-system instrument. Another important design tradition developed in France.

Composers sometimes give the bassoon funny, bouncing tunes, but it is much more than the orchestra’s comedian. It can sound tender, mysterious or grand. In Peter and the Wolf, Prokofiev uses it for Grandfather. In The Rite of Spring, Stravinsky begins with a bassoon playing unusually high. Listen to both: how can the same wooden instrument suggest such different characters?

WoodwindMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Contrabassoon

The woodwind family’s rumbling giant

In a few notes

  • Section: Woodwind.
  • How it sounds: A very long folded double-reed tube; deep, reedy notes.
  • When it began: Contrabassoons developed from earlier double-reed basses in the 1600s and 1700s; the Heckel workshop helped establish the modern form in the late 1800s.
  • Players to know: Susan Nigro and orchestral specialist Lewis Lipnick.
  • A surprise: Its written notes usually sound an octave lower than they look.

The story

If a bassoon is a folded wooden tube, a contrabassoon is a much longer tube folded several times. It curls back on itself so that the player can reach the keys. A floor support carries much of its weight. This is the lowest regular member of the orchestral woodwind family.

The sound begins with a double reed, larger than a bassoon’s. Breath makes the two pieces of cane vibrate, and the long air column answers with very low notes. Down near the bottom of its range, you may hear a grainy rumble, almost as though individual vibrations were peeping through.

Very low bassoon relatives developed during the 1600s and 1700s. Early designs varied greatly, and there was no single inventor of every version. In the late 1800s, the Heckel workshop helped establish a more practical modern form. Makers have continued to improve its keys and response.

The contrabassoon does not appear in every orchestral piece. When a composer wants extra depth, it can strengthen a low line played by cellos, basses or bassoons. It sometimes gets an amusing or surprising solo as well. Listen carefully beneath the busy upper instruments. Can you follow its slow-moving path? A quiet low note may change the feeling of a whole chord without asking everyone to look its way.

WoodwindOccasional guestAbout 2 min read aloud

Saxophone

A golden-coloured woodwind guest

In a few notes

  • Section: Woodwind · An occasional orchestral guest.
  • How it sounds: Single reed and a widening metal tube; flexible, rich and bright.
  • When it began: Adolphe Sax developed the saxophone in the early 1840s and patented the family in 1846.
  • Players to know: Marcel Mule, Claude Delangle, Charlie Parker and John Coltrane.
  • A surprise: It is usually made of brass, but its reed places it in the woodwind family.

The story

This golden instrument is a visitor to the symphony orchestra, rather than a member needed in every piece. The saxophone is famous in jazz and bands, but composers also invite it into classical music. Ravel gives it memorable solos in Boléro, where its unusual colour stands out.

A saxophone is normally made from brass. So why is it a woodwind? Its sound begins with a single reed vibrating against a mouthpiece, much like a clarinet’s. A trumpet begins with vibrating lips instead. The way an instrument makes sound helps decide its family, even when its material suggests something else.

Adolphe Sax, a Belgian maker working in Paris, developed saxophones in the early 1840s and patented the family in 1846. He designed several sizes with different ranges. The alto and tenor are especially familiar, but there are both smaller and much larger relatives.

The player blows through the mouthpiece and presses keys along the widening tube. Changing the breath and mouth shape helps shape a huge variety of sounds. A classical saxophone can sing smoothly and gently; a jazz player may growl, bend notes or make a tune swing. Listen to two different performances and compare their voices. The instrument is the same kind of sound-maker, but each musician tells a different story.

WoodwindMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Recorder

One family, from tiny pipes to tall giants

In a few notes

  • Section: Woodwind.
  • How it sounds: Breath passes through a windway and meets an edge; clear, direct and singing.
  • When it began: Recorders are documented in medieval Europe. The familiar three-piece Baroque design developed in the later 1600s.
  • Players to know: Frans Brüggen, Michala Petri, Piers Adams, Lucie Horsch and Sarah Jeffery.
  • A surprise: Common sizes include sopranino, soprano (descant), alto (treble), tenor and bass. Great bass and contrabass instruments go still lower.

The story

You may have met a recorder at school, but that small instrument is only one member of a much larger family. A tiny sopranino can sound very high. The familiar soprano, also called descant, comes next. Alto, or treble, recorders sound lower, followed by tenor and bass. There are even great bass and contrabass recorders!

The player blows through a mouthpiece with a narrow windway inside. The windway directs air towards a sharp edge. The air begins vibrating, and fingers opening or closing holes help choose the notes. A thumb hole on the back gives the player extra control. Bigger instruments may need keys or a bent blowing tube.

Recorders were played in medieval Europe. During the Renaissance, different sizes often played together in groups called consorts. In the later 1600s, makers developed the three-piece Baroque design. Composers such as Vivaldi and Telemann wrote exciting solo music for the instrument, long before plastic classroom recorders existed.

A recorder can be gentle, nimble or surprisingly powerful. Wooden and plastic instruments both make real music; good breath control matters more than simply blowing harder. Listen to a professional soloist, then a group of different sizes. Can you follow the highest voice while the lower recorders support it? This familiar school instrument has a whole extended family waiting to be heard.

WoodwindOccasional guestAbout 1 min read aloud

Heckelphone

A rare, deep cousin of the oboe

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Woodwind · An occasional orchestral guest.
  • How it sounds: A double reed and wooden tube; a full, low oboe-family voice.
  • When it began: Wilhelm Heckel and his family developed this instrument in Germany; it was presented in 1904.
  • Players to know: Peter Hurd and Robert Howe have helped champion the instrument.
  • A surprise: It sounds an octave below an oboe and often rests on a small support peg.

The story

Take the singing voice of an oboe and imagine a larger, deeper cousin. The heckelphone uses a double reed: two thin blades vibrate together as the player blows. A wide wooden tube and a rounded bell help give it a rich sound.

The Heckel family developed it in Germany and first presented it in 1904. It sounds an octave below the ordinary oboe. A small peg can support the instrument, so the musician does not have to hold all its weight in the hands.

Richard Strauss used the heckelphone in some orchestral works, and Paul Hindemith wrote a trio for heckelphone, viola and piano. It is a rare orchestral guest. Although the bass oboe reaches a similar range, the two are distinct instruments. Listen to its low tune: does it remind you of an oboe, a bassoon or a new voice altogether?

BrassMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Horn (French horn)

A forest call curled into a circle

In a few notes

  • Section: Brass.
  • How it sounds: Buzzing lips in a mouthpiece; rounded, mellow and heroic.
  • When it began: Orchestral horns grew from hunting horns in the 1600s and 1700s. Valves were developed in the early 1800s.
  • Players to know: Dennis Brain, Barry Tuckwell, Sarah Willis and Radek Baborák.
  • A surprise: Horn players usually place their right hand inside the bell to help shape the sound and tuning.

The story

Imagine unrolling a horn’s shining circles into one long tube. There is far more tubing than the neat round shape first suggests! The wide opening at the end is called the bell. The musician holds the instrument with the left hand on the valves and the right hand inside that bell.

The sound starts with the player’s lips buzzing into a small cup-shaped mouthpiece. The horn makes that vibration into a rich musical voice. Valves send air through different lengths of tubing to help choose notes. Breath and lip control are just as important as moving the fingers.

The orchestral horn grew from instruments used for hunting calls in the 1600s and 1700s. Early horns had no valves, so players changed notes using their lips, different tube lengths and, later, hand positions. Valves arrived in the early 1800s and gave musicians more possibilities. The modern double horn combines two sets of tubing.

Horn players can sound like a distant voice in a forest, a warm choir or a team of brave adventurers. Their sound blends especially well with both woodwinds and other brass. Listen to a Mozart horn concerto and notice the playful leaps. Then hear a loud orchestral passage. Can you recognise the same rounded voice when it grows much stronger?

The Bible mentions animal-horn instruments such as the shofar. They are much simpler relatives of lip-buzzed wind instruments, rather than modern orchestral horns with valves.

Trumpet

A bright voice that can whisper too

In a few notes

  • Section: Brass.
  • How it sounds: Buzzing lips and a metal tube; brilliant, clear notes.
  • When it began: Trumpets have ancient ancestors thousands of years old. Valved trumpets developed during the early 1800s.
  • Players to know: Louis Armstrong, Maurice André, Alison Balsom and Wynton Marsalis.
  • A surprise: A mute placed in the bell can change the trumpet’s colour as well as its loudness.

The story

A trumpet can announce a royal arrival with a bright fanfare, but it can also play a soft, thoughtful tune. Its shining tube bends around so the player can comfortably hold it. At one end is a mouthpiece; at the other, the tube opens into a flared bell.

The player buzzes their lips into the mouthpiece. Changing that buzz and the breath produces different notes. Most modern orchestral trumpets have three valves. Each valve redirects the air through extra tubing, helping the player reach notes that a simple open tube cannot easily supply.

Trumpet-like instruments are thousands of years old. People used them for ceremonies and signals long before the modern orchestra existed. Early European orchestral trumpets had no valves. In the early 1800s, makers developed useful valved instruments, greatly increasing the notes players could use. Modern orchestras use trumpets in several sizes and tunings.

A trumpet player may put a mute into the bell to change the sound. One mute can make the voice thin and pointed; another can make it seem distant. In jazz, trumpeters have explored still more colours and ways to bend a tune. Listen for a short trumpet call, then a longer melody. What changes when the instrument stops announcing and begins to sing?

Numbers 10 describes silver trumpets used to call the community together. These were ancient signalling instruments, without the valves of a modern orchestral trumpet. The Bible also mentions animal-horn instruments such as the shofar, a more distant cousin of modern brass instruments.

BrassMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Trombone

The instrument with a moving arm

In a few notes

  • Section: Brass.
  • How it sounds: Buzzing lips; a sliding tube changes the notes.
  • When it began: The slide trombone developed in Europe in the 1400s. Earlier English examples are often called sackbuts.
  • Players to know: Christian Lindberg, Jörgen van Rijen, Carol Jarvis and J. J. Johnson.
  • A surprise: Sliding smoothly between notes makes a glissando: a musical swoop.

The story

Most brass players press valves, but a trombonist has a different tool: a long slide. Push it away and the tube becomes longer. Bring it back and the tube becomes shorter. Changing the length helps change the note. Watch carefully so you do not miss the player’s quick movements.

As with a trumpet or horn, the sound starts with buzzing lips in a mouthpiece. The slide does not do all the work. The musician also controls breath and lip tension, choosing notes that belong to different positions. Some trombones have an extra valve that opens another length of tubing.

The slide trombone developed in Europe in the 1400s. In English, earlier instruments are often called sackbuts. They played in towns, courts and churches long before trombones became regular members of symphony orchestras. The basic slide idea has survived for hundreds of years, even though bells, bores and musical uses have changed.

Trombones can make grand, weighty chords, gentle singing lines and comic swoops. A smooth slide between notes is called a glissando. Composers do not always want a swoop, though: players learn to move the slide so ordinary notes sound cleanly separated. Listen to a trombone melody and notice how a player can make a very mechanical-looking movement produce something as smooth as a singing voice.

Earlier trombones, often called sackbuts, supported church choirs in parts of Europe. Later composers, including J. S. Bach, also used trombones to reinforce sacred choral music.

The deeper voice: bass trombone

A bass trombone plays the low part of the trombone team. Modern instruments usually have a wider bore, a larger bell and one or two valves for extra tubing. Many are still based on the same B-flat tube length as a tenor trombone: the big difference is how comfortably they reach low notes and the weight of their sound. Low trombones have a long history, while today’s valve-equipped designs developed especially during the 1800s and 1900s. Listen to players such as George Roberts and Douglas Yeo.

Tuba

The brass family’s deep foundation

In a few notes

  • Section: Brass.
  • How it sounds: Buzzing lips through a wide mouthpiece; deep, rounded notes.
  • When it began: Wilhelm Wieprecht and Johann Gottfried Moritz patented a bass tuba in Berlin in 1835; later makers developed other sizes.
  • Players to know: Arnold Jacobs, John Fletcher, Roger Bobo and Øystein Baadsvik.
  • A surprise: A large-looking tuba can play quick, light notes as well as slow, heavy ones.

The story

The tuba looks like a great shining bundle of tubing with a bell opening towards the ceiling. It is the lowest regular member of the orchestral brass family. A player sits with it supported on the lap or a stand and blows through a large cup-shaped mouthpiece.

The sound begins with the musician’s lips buzzing. Air travels through a long, widening tube, and valves add extra lengths to help choose notes. Tubas come in several sizes and tunings, so two instruments may look slightly different. Bigger is not always the whole story: the shape and length of the tubing matter too.

Compared with the trumpet’s ancient ancestors, the tuba is quite young. In Berlin in 1835, Wilhelm Wieprecht and Johann Gottfried Moritz patented an important bass tuba design. Other makers then developed larger and different instruments. Composers gained a useful new low voice for bands and orchestras.

In a symphony, the tuba often supports the other brass, giving a strong foundation to a chord. But it is much more nimble than its size suggests. A skilled soloist can make it dance, leap and sing gently. Listen to Vaughan Williams’s Tuba Concerto and follow the main tune. Does this big instrument sound like the slow, clumsy giant you might have expected?

BrassMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Cornet

The trumpet’s rounder-voiced cousin

In a few notes

  • Section: Brass.
  • How it sounds: Buzzing lips, valves and a widening tube; rounded and bright.
  • When it began: The cornet developed in France during the 1820s as makers added valves to compact horn-like instruments.
  • Players to know: Jean-Baptiste Arban, Herbert L. Clarke, Bix Beiderbecke and Philip McCann.
  • A surprise: A usual B-flat cornet and B-flat trumpet can play much the same notes, despite their different shapes.

The story

A cornet looks rather like a trumpet that has curled itself into a smaller bundle. Its tube widens more steadily, and its mouthpiece is usually deeper. Those details help give it a rounded voice. It can still sound bright and exciting, especially when a player launches into quick notes.

The player buzzes the lips into a mouthpiece and presses valves to change the route through the tubing. Although a cornet looks shorter than a trumpet, its tube is folded differently. A usual B-flat cornet and B-flat trumpet have similar tubing lengths and can share much of the same musical range.

The cornet developed in France during the 1820s as makers experimented with adding valves to compact horn-like instruments. Its flexible voice became popular with virtuoso soloists and brass bands. Composers also invited it into orchestras when they wanted its particular colour alongside, or instead of, trumpets.

In a British-style brass band, cornets often carry the leading melodies. Early jazz players also loved them. Listen to a cornet solo, then compare it with a trumpet. Both can sing, sparkle and leap, so the difference is not simply loud versus quiet. Try imagining two people saying the same sentence in slightly different voices. Which sound would you choose for a gentle song, and which for a lively announcement?

BrassOccasional guestAbout 2 min read aloud

Euphonium

A warm voice from the brass band

In a few notes

  • Section: Brass · An occasional orchestral guest.
  • How it sounds: Buzzing lips and valves; a mellow tenor-and-bass voice.
  • When it began: The euphonium developed in the 1840s. A design made by Ferdinand Sommer in Weimar in 1843 is commonly credited as an important early example.
  • Players to know: Simone Mantia, Steven Mead, David Childs and Demondrae Thurman.
  • A surprise: Its name comes from Greek words meaning “sweet-sounding” or “well-sounding”.

The story

Imagine a small tuba with a warm, singing voice. That is a useful first picture of a euphonium, though it is an instrument with its own character. Its name is pronounced “yoo-foh-nee-um”. It belongs to the brass family and is especially at home in brass bands and wind bands.

The player buzzes the lips into a mouthpiece. Valves send air through extra lengths of tubing to change the notes. Many euphoniums have four valves, though three-valve versions exist too. The tube widens along much of its journey, helping create the rounded tone. The instrument is related to the baritone horn, but the names do not always mean exactly the same design.

The euphonium developed during the 1840s, after valves made low brass instruments more flexible. Ferdinand Sommer’s instrument, made in Weimar in 1843, is often named as an important early example. Other makers continued to refine the shape and valve systems.

It is an occasional orchestral guest rather than a regular member of every symphony. Sometimes a part labelled tenor tuba is played on euphonium, depending on the music and performance tradition. As a soloist, it can sing a long melody or race through astonishingly quick passages. Listen without looking at its size: does the sound seem heavier, lighter or more agile than you expected?

BrassOccasional guestAbout 2 min read aloud

Sousaphone

A tuba that wraps around its player

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Brass · An occasional orchestral guest.
  • How it sounds: Buzzing lips and valves; a deep bass voice made for bands.
  • When it began: J. W. Pepper built an early sousaphone in 1893 for John Philip Sousa. Later makers developed the familiar forward-facing bell.
  • Players to know: Kirk Joseph, Nat McIntosh and many marching-band and New Orleans brass-band musicians.
  • A surprise: The earliest upright bells were nicknamed rain-catchers.

The story

A sousaphone carries a deep tuba-like voice around its player’s body. The long tube coils into a large ring, and the bell rises above the musician. Valves change the route through the tube, while buzzing lips begin the sound.

Bandleader John Philip Sousa wanted a useful low instrument for his band. J. W. Pepper built an early sousaphone in 1893. Its bell pointed upward. Later instruments often had a forward-facing bell, helping send the sound towards an audience during a march.

The sousaphone belongs to the brass family. It is especially at home in marching bands and New Orleans brass bands, rather than the usual symphony orchestra. Some bodies are brass; others use lighter fibreglass. Listen beneath the tune for a bouncy bass line. Can you imagine walking in step with those low notes?

A sousaphone and a concert tuba share much of their musical job: both can provide the foundation beneath higher brass. Their shapes suit different situations. A seated orchestral player can support a tuba on the lap, while a marching player needs a way to carry the tube. In a New Orleans ensemble, the sousaphone may create a busy, playful bass pattern rather than simply holding long notes.

PercussionMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Timpani

Drums that know their notes

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion.
  • How it sounds: Large bowl-shaped drums with definite pitches; played with padded beaters.
  • When it began: Kettledrums have medieval and earlier ancestors. They entered European orchestral life in the 1600s; pedal mechanisms developed in the 1800s.
  • Players to know: Saul Goodman, Vic Firth, David Herbert and timpanist-percussionist Evelyn Glennie.
  • A surprise: The singular word is timpano; a set of drums is called timpani.

The story

At the back of an orchestra you may see a row of huge copper-coloured bowls. A tightly stretched head covers each bowl. These are timpani, also called kettledrums. Unlike many drums, each can make a clear musical pitch: a note you could try to hum.

The timpanist strikes the head with beaters that often have soft coverings. Different beaters and playing positions change the colour of the sound. A pedal changes the head’s tension, allowing the player to tune the drum. The player must listen very carefully, sometimes changing notes while other musicians continue around them.

Kettledrums have a long history in different cultures, including instruments carried with military groups. They became established in European orchestras during the 1600s, often alongside trumpets. Pedal-tuning mechanisms developed in the 1800s. There was no single inventor of every kind of kettledrum.

Timpani can make a quiet rumble, a sharp musical punctuation mark or an enormous rolling thunder. To make a roll, the player alternates quick strokes so that the sound seems continuous. The timpanist also stops vibrations with the hands when the music needs silence. Listen for an important low note in a dramatic passage. Is the drum simply keeping time, or is its pitch helping the whole orchestra tell the story?

PercussionMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Snare drum

The drum with a secret rattle

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion.
  • How it sounds: A struck drumhead with rattling wires underneath; crisp and sharp.
  • When it began: European snare drums developed from medieval tabor traditions, with military side drums becoming important from the late Middle Ages onwards.
  • Players to know: Jacques Delécluse, Evelyn Glennie and percussionist David Corkhill. Many jazz drummers, including Buddy Rich, also play snare drum.
  • A surprise: The “snares” are the wires beneath the drum, not the sticks used to play it.

The story

Tap an ordinary drumhead and it goes “dum”. Add a row of fine wires against the lower head and the sound becomes a crisp “rrat”! Those wires are called snares. They vibrate when the top head is struck, adding the rattle that gives the snare drum its name.

An orchestral player usually uses two wooden sticks, though other tools can make different sounds. Tiny, controlled strokes can be very quiet. Fast alternating or bouncing strokes make a roll, a sound that can keep going almost without gaps. A lever lets the player move the snares away from the lower head.

The snare drum grew from earlier drums such as the medieval tabor. Military side drums became important in Europe during the late Middle Ages and afterwards, helping groups march and carry signals. Modern orchestral drums gained improved tension systems and metal wires over a long period. There is no single inventor to name.

In an orchestra, a snare drum can make a march snap into life or build excitement under a repeated pattern. Ravel’s Boléro gives it an exceptionally patient job: keeping a little rhythm going while the orchestral colours change. Listen to that pattern without trying to hear the whole piece at once. Can a repeated rhythm remain steady while everything around it grows?

PercussionMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Bass drum

A great round voice for musical thunder

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion.
  • How it sounds: A very large drumhead struck with a beater; deep, booming sounds.
  • When it began: Large drums have ancient roots. Turkish-style military bass drums influenced European orchestras during the 1700s.
  • Players to know: Percussionists Evelyn Glennie, David Corkhill and Colin Currie play bass drum among many instruments.
  • A surprise: An orchestral bass drum is usually much larger than the bass drum in a rock drum kit.

The story

The orchestral bass drum is a giant round instrument, often hanging in a frame so the player can reach it easily. A large head stretches across each side of its shell. Strike it with a padded beater and the room may fill with a deep boom. A gentle touch can make a soft, shadowy sound instead.

Unlike timpani, a bass drum is not usually asked to play a precise note from a tune. Its job is often about colour, weight and rhythm. The player chooses a beater and a place to strike, then carefully controls how long the vibration lasts. A hand can stop a boom before it muddies the next musical moment.

Large drums have existed in many cultures for centuries, so the bass drum has no single inventor. During the 1700s, European composers became interested in the sounds of Turkish military bands. Bass drums, cymbals and triangles helped bring those colours into orchestral music.

A bass drum can suggest a distant storm or give one powerful beat that makes everybody sit up. In quiet music it may be felt almost as much as heard. Watch the player waiting between notes: a single stroke must arrive at exactly the right time. Can you notice how silence makes the next great boom seem even larger?

PercussionMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Cymbals

Two shining plates, a thousand colours

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion.
  • How it sounds: Metal discs struck together or played with beaters; shimmering and crashing.
  • When it began: Cymbals have ancient roots in Asia and the Middle East. Turkish cymbal-making influenced European orchestras in the 1700s.
  • Players to know: Percussionists Evelyn Glennie, David Corkhill and Colin Currie; jazz drummer Tony Williams also explored cymbal sounds.
  • A surprise: For a quiet shimmer, a player can roll on one suspended cymbal with soft beaters.

The story

A cymbal looks like a round metal plate with a raised centre. Orchestras use several kinds. For a crash, the player brings two cymbals together. For a suspended cymbal, a single disc hangs from a stand and is struck with a stick or a soft beater.

The metal vibrates in many ways at once. That makes a rich mixture of sounds rather than one simple note you can easily sing. A player can let the sound ring or bring the cymbals against the body to stop it. Timing the end of a crash matters as much as timing the beginning.

Cymbals have ancient histories in Asia and the Middle East. There is no single person who invented them all. The skilled work of Turkish cymbal makers helped shape the sounds European orchestras adopted during the 1700s. Modern cymbals come in different metal mixtures, sizes, shapes and thicknesses.

Although cymbals are famous for enormous crashes, they can be wonderfully quiet. Soft beaters rolled on a suspended cymbal make a shimmer that seems to grow out of nowhere. Composers use that colour for magic, suspense and waves of excitement. Listen for the start of a cymbal sound and then follow its fading tail. How long can you hear it after the player has stopped striking?

Psalm 150 includes cymbals among instruments used in praise. Ancient cymbals and modern orchestral cymbals share the idea of ringing metal, though their sizes and shapes need not match.

PercussionMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Triangle

A small sparkle that travels far

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion.
  • How it sounds: A metal rod struck with a metal beater; bright, ringing overtones.
  • When it began: Metal triangles are shown in medieval European art. Their familiar orchestral role grew during the 1700s.
  • Players to know: Orchestral percussionists such as David Corkhill and Colin Currie play triangle alongside many other instruments.
  • A surprise: The open corner helps the metal vibrate freely; the player hangs it from a small loop.

The story

A triangle looks like one of the simplest objects in the orchestra: a metal rod bent into three sides, with one corner left open. It hangs from a small loop. Strike it with a metal beater and its bright sound can sparkle right through a large group of musicians.

Holding the metal itself would stop much of the vibration. That is why the suspension loop matters. A percussionist can also touch the triangle deliberately to shorten a note. To make a roll, the player moves a beater quickly between two sides. Making a soft, even roll takes far more practice than the little instrument’s shape suggests.

Metal triangles appear in medieval European pictures. Some early versions had jingling rings attached. The familiar instrument became more important in orchestras during the 1700s, especially with music inspired by Turkish military-band sounds. Its long history does not give us one reliable inventor or birthday.

In Liszt’s First Piano Concerto, the triangle has such a noticeable part that listeners gave the piece a teasing nickname: the “Triangle Concerto”. It is still a piano concerto, but the tiny percussion voice gets its moment! Listen for that bright ping. Does it change the music’s mood even when the note lasts only a little while?

PercussionMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Tambourine

A drum wearing a necklace of jingles

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion.
  • How it sounds: A frame drum with metal jingles; tapped, shaken or rubbed.
  • When it began: Frame drums have existed for thousands of years. Jingle-equipped tambourines developed in several traditions; orchestras adopted them especially in the 1700s and 1800s.
  • Players to know: Percussionists Evelyn Glennie, David Corkhill and Glen Velez, a specialist in frame drums.
  • A surprise: A skilled player can make a roll by rubbing a thumb along the drumhead.

The story

The tambourine is two sound-makers sharing one frame. A stretched drumhead gives a small thump, while pairs of metal discs around the edge jingle and chatter. Some tambourines have no head at all. Shake one and the metal discs still make a cheerful sound.

Orchestral percussionists use careful finger and hand movements to control both sounds. They may tap with the fingertips, shake the frame or rub a thumb across the head to make the jingles roll. Playing a very quiet, even rhythm can be tricky: the metal pieces want to move and sound whenever the instrument moves.

Frame drums have been played for thousands of years across different cultures. Versions with jingles developed in more than one place, so there is no single inventor of the tambourine family. European orchestras used tambourines increasingly during the 1700s and 1800s, often to suggest dancing and colourful celebrations.

Listen to a dance with tambourine and try to separate the head’s little taps from the bright metal chatter. Sometimes the player makes a rhythm that answers the melody; sometimes a shake supplies a continuous sparkling background. An instrument that seems easy to pick up can offer a whole world of small choices. What happens to a familiar tune when you add a gentle jingle on its strongest beats?

Exodus 15:20 describes Miriam leading women with timbrels or hand drums and dancing. This is a close ancient relative of the tambourine family; we cannot assume it had exactly the same jingles as a modern tambourine.

PercussionMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Xylophone

Wooden steps for a dancing tune

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion.
  • How it sounds: Tuned wooden bars struck with mallets; clear, dry and quick.
  • When it began: Wooden-bar instruments have long histories in Africa and Asia. The European orchestral xylophone became prominent during the 1800s.
  • Players to know: George Hamilton Green, Yoichi Hiraoka and percussionist Evelyn Glennie.
  • A surprise: Its name comes from Greek words meaning “wood sound”.

The story

The xylophone is a row of wooden bars waiting to turn into a tune. Its bars are arranged rather like the white and black keys of a piano. A player strikes them with mallets. Each carefully shaped bar vibrates at a particular pitch, so this percussion instrument can play melodies.

Longer bars usually make lower notes. Tubes beneath the bars help strengthen the sound. The mallet heads matter too: hard ones make a sharp, bright attack. In an orchestra the xylophone often sounds dry and quick, with notes that leap out and then fade. A marimba is a related wooden-bar instrument with a different range and character.

Wooden-bar instruments have long histories in both Africa and Asia. Their stories cannot be reduced to a single European inventor. Travelling performers helped make the xylophone familiar to European audiences during the 1800s. Composers then found exciting uses for it in orchestras.

Saint-Saëns used a xylophone in Danse macabre, where its rattling notes can suggest dancing bones. That is a musical picture, not the material the instrument is made from! Other pieces give it racing, playful tunes. Watch the player move between bars: the notes are spread across a wide space, and a fast melody needs accurate aim. Can you tap the rhythm without trying to play every note?

PercussionMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Glockenspiel

A pocketful of silver stars

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion.
  • How it sounds: Tuned metal bars and hard mallets; very high, bell-like notes.
  • When it began: The instrument grew from European tuned-bell traditions. Metal-bar forms developed over the 1600s and 1700s and later entered orchestral use.
  • Players to know: Percussionists Evelyn Glennie, Colin Currie and David Corkhill play glockenspiel among many instruments.
  • A surprise: Glockenspiel is German for “bell play”; its orchestral notes sound two octaves above the written notes.

The story

A glockenspiel looks a little like a tiny xylophone, but its bars are metal rather than wood. Strike a bar with a hard mallet and it rings with a bright, bell-like sound. Its small size does not stop those high notes from shining through an orchestra.

The bars are arranged in two rows, like a piano keyboard. Each bar is tuned to a particular note, so a percussionist can play a melody. The player must aim carefully and think about how long the ringing notes should continue. Too many notes left ringing can blur a musical pattern.

The name comes from German words meaning “bell play”. Earlier instruments used sets of real bells. Metal-bar versions developed in Europe over the 1600s and 1700s, and orchestral designs continued to change. No one inventor created every stage of that journey. Some historic keyboard-operated instruments could play similar bright sounds.

In modern orchestral writing, the glockenspiel usually sounds two octaves higher than the notes written for the player. Composers use its sparkle for magic, playfulness or an extra flash of light above a melody. Listen to it beside a xylophone. Both have rows of bars, but can you hear the difference between the metal’s ringing tail and the wood’s much shorter, drier voice?

PercussionMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Tubular bells

Church-bell sounds that fit on a stage

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion.
  • How it sounds: Hanging metal tubes struck near the top; tuned bell-like notes.
  • When it began: Orchestral tubular bells developed during the late 1800s; English maker John Harrington patented a design in 1884.
  • Players to know: Orchestral percussionists including David Corkhill and Evelyn Glennie play tubular bells among many instruments.
  • A surprise: The player strikes the tops of the tubes, even though much of each tube hangs far below.

The story

How could an orchestra bring a whole church tower onto a concert stage? It cannot, but tubular bells offer a useful answer. Long metal tubes hang from a frame. Strike a tube near its top with a special hammer and the result suggests a large ringing bell.

Different tube lengths make different pitches. The tubes are arranged in a keyboard-like pattern, so the player can choose a tune or a chord. A damper helps stop them ringing. Without that control, yesterday’s musical note might seem to hang around while the next one arrives!

Orchestral tubular bells developed during the late 1800s as a practical alternative to sets of enormous bells. Several makers worked on related designs. In England, John Harrington patented a version in 1884. Because the instrument evolved through different experiments, its story is better told as a period of development than one simple moment of invention.

Composers use tubular bells to suggest ceremonies, midnight clocks, celebrations and distant towers. They can sound grand, mysterious or even slightly frightening, depending on what the other instruments are doing. Listen to a passage with bells and imagine taking them away. Would the scene still feel the same? Watch where the player strikes: a very long tube can be set ringing by one small, well-placed movement near the top.

Orchestral scores sometimes call tubular bells “chimes”. The tiny, high, sparkling instrument in this guide has its own card: Bar chimes (mark tree). These are different instruments. Outdoor wind chimes ring when moving air sets their parts in motion.

PercussionMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Tam-tam

A great bronze circle full of mystery

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion.
  • How it sounds: A large suspended metal disc; a spreading wash of sound without one clear note.
  • When it began: Flat metal gongs have long Asian histories. Tam-tams entered European orchestral music around the end of the 1700s.
  • Players to know: Percussionists Evelyn Glennie, David Corkhill and Colin Currie.
  • A surprise: A tam-tam is a kind of gong, usually fairly flat and without a raised central boss.

The story

A great metal disc hangs at the back of the orchestra. A percussionist lifts a padded beater and touches it into sound. At first there may be a dark murmur. Then a spreading shimmer grows, filling the air with layers of vibration. This instrument is called a tam-tam.

People often call it a gong. More precisely, a tam-tam is generally a fairly flat gong without the raised central knob found on many pitched Asian gongs. It does not usually offer one clear note to sing. Instead, its many vibrations create a complex wash of sound.

Gongs have long and varied histories in Asia. Different communities developed instruments with different shapes, tunings and musical jobs. European orchestras began using tam-tams around the end of the 1700s. The orchestral instrument has no single known inventor, and its story belongs within that much larger family of traditions.

A tam-tam can make a frightening crash or a sound so soft it seems to arrive from very far away. The size of the instrument, the beater and the strength of the stroke all matter. The player may also warm it into vibration before an important note. Listen to the sound after the strike: does it stay the same, or slowly change as some vibrations fade before others?

PercussionMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Marimba

Wooden bars with a deep, warm glow

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion.
  • How it sounds: Tuned wooden bars over resonator tubes, struck with mallets; warm and rounded.
  • When it began: Marimbas have African roots and important histories in Central America. The modern concert instrument developed during the late 1800s and 1900s.
  • Players to know: Keiko Abe, Leigh Howard Stevens, Nancy Zeltsman and Evelyn Glennie.
  • A surprise: Many players hold four mallets at once, allowing them to play chords and several musical lines.

The story

A marimba looks like a large wooden keyboard on legs. Beneath the bars hang tubes of different lengths. A player strikes the bars with mallets, and the tubes help strengthen the sound. Long bars usually make low notes. Their warm ring is different from the shorter, brighter sound of an orchestral xylophone.

Many marimba players hold two mallets in each hand. By changing the distance between the mallets, they can play chords, a tune with an accompaniment, or widely spaced notes. To keep a note sounding, the player may make a gentle roll, repeating strokes so the separate attacks blend together.

The marimba’s story has African roots and important chapters in Central America, especially Guatemala and Mexico. African musical traditions travelled to the Americas with people forced into slavery. Local communities developed their own instruments and playing traditions. Wooden resonators and later metal tubes helped shape modern concert instruments during the late 1800s and 1900s.

Today the marimba is heard in solo concerts, percussion ensembles, bands and some orchestral pieces. It is especially important in music written after the usual common-practice era. Listen to a low, quiet phrase, then a quick dance. Can the same rows of wooden bars suggest a calm voice one moment and a whole busy group the next?

PercussionMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Wood block

A hollow piece of wood with a sharp little voice

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion.
  • How it sounds: A hollow wooden block struck with a stick; dry, sharp clicks.
  • When it began: Slit drums have long histories in several cultures. The compact orchestral wood block became familiar in Western ensembles during the late 1800s and early 1900s.
  • Players to know: Percussionists David Corkhill, Evelyn Glennie and Colin Currie play wood blocks among many other instruments.
  • A surprise: The slit and hollow space help a small block of wood produce a surprisingly strong sound.

The story

A wood block can look almost too simple to be an instrument. It is a small piece of wood with a slit and a hollow space inside. Tap it with a stick and it makes a clear, dry click. The hollow shape helps the wood’s vibration become easier to hear.

Percussionists choose different sticks and striking places to change the attack. Blocks also come in different sizes, giving higher or lower colours. The notes do not usually belong to a carefully tuned melody, but they can make a rhythmic pattern leap out from an orchestra. A short sound leaves lots of room for silence between the beats.

Slit drums have long histories in several cultures. The small wood block familiar in Western orchestras and theatre music became established during the late 1800s and early 1900s. It has connections with Asian wooden percussion and with instruments used by early drummers. Its development cannot be pinned to one reliable inventor and birthday.

Britten includes a wood block in the percussion variation of The Young Person’s Guide to the Orchestra. Listen for a crisp wooden voice among the metal rings and drum sounds. Try copying just its rhythm with your fingertips on your knee. Does the pattern feel different when you leave a bigger space between two notes? A musician can make a great deal happen with a very small sound.

PercussionMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Castanets

Two little shells that chatter together

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion.
  • How it sounds: Pairs of hollowed shells, often wooden, clicked together; crisp and rattling.
  • When it began: Clappers have ancient histories around the Mediterranean. The familiar castanet tradition developed over centuries, especially in Spain.
  • Players to know: Lucero Tena, José de Udaeta and Emma Maleras.
  • A surprise: Dancers can play hand-held castanets, while orchestral players may use instruments mounted on handles or a stand.

The story

Castanets look like little curved shells joined with a cord. Each pair has two hollowed halves. Bring them together and they make a sharp click. Skilled players can turn separate clicks into quick rolls and patterns that seem to chatter, laugh or answer the music.

Hand-held castanets are often tied around the thumbs, leaving the fingers to tap the shells. A dancer can play while moving. In an orchestra, percussionists may use castanets mounted on handles or a stand. That makes them practical to pick up and put down between other instruments. Wood is traditional, though modern makers use other materials too.

Clappers have ancient histories around the Mediterranean, so no single person invented the whole family. The familiar castanet tradition developed over centuries and became especially associated with Spanish music and dance. Different regional traditions have their own techniques and sounds.

Composers use castanets for much more than a simple beat. They can add a dancing colour, a dry little reply or an exciting flourish. Lucero Tena helped show how expressive they can be as a solo instrument with an orchestra. Listen to the contrast between single clicks and a flowing roll. Can you tell when the castanets are keeping the pulse and when they are decorating a tune with their own tiny musical sentences?

PercussionMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Vibraphone

Metal bars with a gently shimmering voice

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion.
  • How it sounds: Tuned metal bars, resonator tubes and mallets; ringing notes with optional pulsing tremolo.
  • When it began: The vibraphone developed in the United States during the 1920s. Makers added rotating fans and a damper pedal to metal-bar designs.
  • Players to know: Lionel Hampton, Milt Jackson, Gary Burton and Evelyn Glennie.
  • A surprise: A small motor can turn discs inside the resonators, making the loudness pulse. Players can also switch that effect off.

The story

The vibraphone has rows of metal bars arranged like a piano keyboard. A player strikes them with mallets, and tubes beneath the bars strengthen the ringing sound. It looks related to the xylophone and marimba, but its metal voice can linger in the air for much longer.

There is a special surprise under the bars. A motor can turn discs near the tops of the resonator tubes, repeatedly opening and closing the air space. That makes the sound pulse in loudness, an effect called tremolo. Despite the instrument’s name, this is not mainly a change in the pitch of the note.

The vibraphone developed in the United States during the 1920s. It is younger than the instruments of the usual common-practice orchestra. Makers improved its resonators and added a pedal-operated damper. Pressing the pedal lets notes ring; releasing it helps stop them. Players also stop individual notes with their hands or mallets.

Jazz musicians made the vibraphone famous, and composers brought it into concert and orchestral music too. Some players use four mallets to build rich chords. Listen first with the motor effect, then without it. The instrument can be dreamy, sharp, rhythmic or very still. How does a musician keep a quick tune clear when yesterday’s notes are still ringing beneath it?

PercussionMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Temple blocks

A small team of hollow wooden voices

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion.
  • How it sounds: Hollow wooden blocks in different sizes, struck with sticks; round, woody knocks.
  • When it began: Temple blocks draw on East Asian wooden slit-drum traditions. Sets entered Western bands and orchestral percussion especially during the early 1900s.
  • Players to know: Percussionists David Corkhill, Evelyn Glennie and Colin Currie play sets of blocks among many instruments.
  • A surprise: A set can give several contrasting high and low sounds without forming an ordinary tuned scale.

The story

Temple blocks are a little team of hollow wooden instruments. Each has a slit that helps the body vibrate and a rounded sound that can seem more hollow than an ordinary rectangular wood block. A percussionist often has several sizes arranged on a stand, ready for quick changes.

The player strikes them with sticks or mallets. Different sizes produce different high and low colours. They are not usually tuned like the notes of a piano, but a pattern can still have a clear shape as it hops between them. The player chooses the beater carefully: a harder one makes a sharper beginning to the sound.

These instruments draw on East Asian wooden slit-drum traditions, including instruments used in religious practice. The names, shapes and uses vary between cultures. Sets of temple blocks became familiar in Western bands, theatre music and orchestral percussion during the early 1900s. It would be misleading to name one person as the inventor of the entire family.

Composers can use the blocks for dancing patterns, quick punctuation or sounds that suggest footsteps and movement. In Leroy Anderson’s Sleigh Ride, temple blocks suggest the clip-clop of a horse’s hooves. Listen for a pattern that repeats, then changes its ending. Could two different wooden knocks tell a small musical joke without playing a single conventional melody note?

PercussionMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Sleigh bells

A handful of winter sparkle

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion.
  • How it sounds: Small enclosed metal bells shaken together; a bright, continuous jingle.
  • When it began: Jingle bells have long histories on clothing, animals and vehicles. Sets became a colourful orchestral effect, especially in music of the 1800s and 1900s.
  • Players to know: Orchestral percussionists such as David Corkhill, Evelyn Glennie and Colin Currie play sleigh bells among many instruments.
  • A surprise: Inside each little bell is a loose pellet that strikes the metal when it moves.

The story

A set of sleigh bells can make a concert hall feel like a snowy outdoor scene. Small metal bells are fixed to a strap or handle. Inside each is a loose pellet. Shake the set and the pellets strike their metal shells, making many bright jingles at once.

An orchestral player must do more than shake as loudly as possible. The movement controls the rhythm, the strength of each jingle and how much sound continues between beats. Stopping cleanly can be surprisingly difficult: little metal pieces want to keep moving after the player’s hand has stopped.

Jingle bells have been used for centuries on clothing, animals and vehicles in different cultures. Bells on a moving sleigh could help people hear it coming. There is no single inventor of the whole bell family. Composers increasingly used sets of them for colourful effects in orchestral music during the 1800s and 1900s.

Mozart’s German Dance known as The Sleigh Ride includes sleigh-bell sounds, and Leroy Anderson later made them famous in his own Sleigh Ride. They need not always mean winter, but that association is very strong. Listen for their steady pattern beneath the tune. Can you keep following the bells while the melody changes? Then imagine the same music without them. How much of the scene disappears?

PercussionMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Maracas (maraca)

A pair of rattles with dancing rhythms

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion.
  • How it sounds: Seeds, beads or other small objects shaken inside a shell; dry rattling rhythms.
  • When it began: Maraca traditions have Indigenous roots in the Americas. Makers and musicians developed many regional forms; orchestral composers used them especially during the 1900s.
  • Players to know: Venezuelan maraqueros such as Máximo Teppa and Juan Ernesto Laya; orchestral percussionists also play maracas.
  • A surprise: A player can make different strokes by controlling when the filling hits the inside of the shell.

The story

Maracas are rattles with a musical secret inside. A hollow shell holds seeds, beads or other small objects. Shake it and the filling strikes the inner walls. Traditional shells may be gourds; modern instruments can also be made from wood, leather or plastic. Each material gives a different kind of chatter.

They are often played as a pair, one in each hand, though playing traditions vary. A skilled player controls the direction, speed and stopping point of each movement. The filling takes a little time to travel, so a clear rhythm depends on knowing exactly when it will meet the shell. Fast, crisp patterns require great control.

Maraca traditions have Indigenous roots in the Americas and developed in many regional forms. They can have ceremonial roles as well as musical ones. There is no single inventor or date for the whole family. During the 1900s, concert composers used maracas to add new colours to orchestras and percussion ensembles.

In Venezuelan joropo music, expert players can make a pair sound like a whole rhythmic conversation. In orchestral music, they may supply a dry shimmer behind other instruments. Listen for repeated strokes and sudden gaps. Does the pattern sound as though it is pushing the tune forward, answering it, or simply keeping everybody dancing together?
