PercussionMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Güiro

A musical rasp made for dancing rhythms

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion.
  • How it sounds: A ridged surface scraped with a stick; short clicks and longer rasping strokes.
  • When it began: The güiro has Indigenous Caribbean roots. Different scraper traditions developed across Latin America, later entering orchestral music especially during the 1900s.
  • Players to know: Enrique Lazaga, a Cuban güiro specialist; orchestral percussionists also play the instrument.
  • A surprise: A long scrape and several short scrapes can make a complete repeating rhythmic pattern.

The story

A güiro makes its voice when you scrape it. The player draws a stick across a row of ridges, creating a dry rasp. A long movement gives a long sound, while a quick little movement gives a short one. Put those sounds in a pattern and the instrument begins to dance.

Many traditional güiros are made from hollow gourds. Some have holes for the player’s fingers, making them easier to hold. Wooden and plastic versions are common too. The related metal güira has its own traditions and sound; not every scraped instrument should be treated as exactly the same kind.

The güiro has Indigenous Caribbean roots and a long history in Latin American music. Different communities developed their own shapes, names and playing patterns. There is no single known inventor or birthday. During the 1900s, composers also used scrapers such as the güiro to give concert music a new rhythmic colour.

In a dance band, the güiro can help keep a groove moving while other musicians play melodies above it. In an orchestra it may appear only when the composer asks for that particular sound. Listen to a long scrape followed by two short ones. Can you keep that pattern steady with your voice? Then hear how the player changes the accents: a simple rasp can have a very lively musical personality.

Rainstick

A little rain shower inside a tube

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion · An occasional orchestral guest.
  • How it sounds: Loose seeds or pebbles tumble through obstacles inside a closed tube.
  • When it began: Rainsticks are associated with South America, but their exact beginnings are disputed. A certain ancient invention date is not established.
  • Players to know: Percussionists, storytellers and community musicians; no single famous player defines this instrument.
  • A surprise: Tilting slowly can make the shower last longer than tipping it straight upright.

The story

Turn a rainstick gently and listen. Inside its closed tube, tiny seeds or pebbles tumble over obstacles. Instead of falling in one quick heap, they trickle through, making a soft rushing sound like rain.

Some examples use dried cactus with thorns pushed inward. Others use bamboo, wood or modern materials. You do not have to strike a note: gravity does much of the work! Changing the angle changes how quickly the filling travels.

Rainsticks are associated with South America, but their early history is uncertain. Stories about one particular ancient inventor or rain-making ceremony are not all securely documented. Today musicians use them for sound pictures and gentle textures. Imagine telling a story with no words: where would you place this little shower?

Cabasa

A twist makes a shimmering scrape

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion · An occasional orchestral guest.
  • How it sounds: Metal bead chains rub against a rough cylinder; a controlled scraping rattle.
  • When it began: Gourd rattles are older relatives. Martin Cohen designed the modern metal-bead Afuche-Cabasa in the 1960s; its US patent dates from 1970.
  • Players to know: Played by Latin-jazz and studio percussionists; Martin Cohen was its designer.
  • A surprise: Twisting and stopping can make more precise rhythms than simply shaking.

The story

A cabasa looks like a small cylinder wearing a coat of shiny beads. Hold its handle and let the other hand rest lightly on the bead chains. Turn the cylinder, and the chains rub against its rough surface. That makes a crisp, sandy rattle.

Older relatives were made with gourds or shells and an outside network of beads. During the 1960s, Martin Cohen developed the sturdy metal-chain Afuche-Cabasa. His design received a United States patent in 1970.

Percussionists use cabasas in Latin music, jazz, recordings and concert ensembles. Turning, shaking and stopping make different patterns. The beads need freedom to move: squeezing them tightly will change the sound. Listen for how a small scraping instrument can help a whole band feel lively.

Chime bar

One bar, one ringing note

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion · An occasional orchestral guest.
  • How it sounds: A mallet strikes one tuned metal bar above a small resonating box.
  • When it began: Separate tuned bars are part of modern classroom percussion, developed alongside twentieth-century music-education instruments.
  • Players to know: Often played by school ensembles and community music groups rather than a particular famous soloist.
  • A surprise: Each player can hold just one note while a whole group shares the tune.

The story

A chime bar is a single tuned metal bar, usually resting above its own little box. Strike it gently with a suitable mallet and hear one clear, ringing note. Put several different bars together and you can build a tune.

Separate chime bars are especially useful in classrooms. One child can look after one note while another answers with a different note. Longer bars usually make lower sounds. The hollow support helps the note speak, rather as a larger instrument body helps a string.

This is a modern teaching instrument, not an ancient instrument with one known inventor. It belongs to the larger metallophone family. It is different from tall orchestral tubular bells and from dangling bar chimes, which make a sparkling sweep.

Anvil

A blacksmith’s tool joins the orchestra

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion · An occasional orchestral guest.
  • How it sounds: A hammer strikes a heavy metal surface; bright, ringing clangs.
  • When it began: Anvils began as metalworking tools. Composers brought their ringing blows into nineteenth-century theatre and orchestral music.
  • Players to know: Usually played by an orchestra’s percussion section, rather than a specialist anvil soloist.
  • A surprise: Concert players may use carefully chosen metal blocks instead of a full blacksmith’s anvil.

The story

An anvil is usually a blacksmith’s tool: a strong metal block on which heated metal can be shaped. In music, the ring of a hammer blow becomes a dramatic percussion sound. A concert anvil might be a specially chosen metal block instead of the enormous tool in a workshop.

During the nineteenth century, composers used anvil sounds to suggest workers and busy forges. Wagner’s operas and Verdi’s famous Anvil Chorus helped make that ringing rhythm familiar in theatres.

The player must choose the right metal, hammer and striking place for the sound the composer wants. There may be more than one pitch. Listen for the way a workman’s repeated action becomes part of the musical beat. The orchestra can tell a story using tools as well as purpose-built instruments!

PercussionOccasional guestAbout 1 min read aloud

Claves

Two sticks with an important musical job

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion · An occasional orchestral guest.
  • How it sounds: Two hard wooden sticks strike together; a bright, hollow click.
  • When it began: Claves developed within Cuban musical traditions; their familiar role grew with nineteenth- and twentieth-century Afro-Cuban ensemble music.
  • Players to know: Afro-Cuban and salsa percussionists, including musicians in the Tito Puente Orchestra.
  • A surprise: Clave also names a repeating rhythmic pattern: the instrument and the pattern are not quite the same thing.

The story

Claves may look like two simple wooden sticks, but their sound can organise a whole band. One stick rests loosely in a cupped hand. The other strikes it, making a clear click that travels through the musical texture.

The instrument is closely connected with Cuban music. The word clave also names important repeating rhythmic patterns. In salsa and related styles, other musical parts fit around these patterns, rather like the pieces of a moving puzzle.

Claves have no single securely recorded invention date. They became familiar through Afro-Cuban music and later travelled into orchestras, classrooms and many kinds of bands. Holding the lower stick too tightly muffles its ring. Listen first to the wooden clicks, then to the whole ensemble: can you still feel that pattern underneath?

PercussionOccasional guestAbout 1 min read aloud

Cowbell

A farmyard signal becomes a musical voice

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion · An occasional orchestral guest.
  • How it sounds: A hollow metal bell struck with a stick; firm, cutting knocks.
  • When it began: Animal bells have existed for centuries. Musical cowbells developed in several traditions, including Afro-Cuban music and European orchestral music.
  • Players to know: Tito Puente and many Latin-music percussionists; orchestral players also use tuned Alpine bells.
  • A surprise: Many musical cowbells have no swinging clapper inside: the player supplies the strikes.

The story

Before joining a band, a cowbell helped people hear where an animal was grazing. Bells hung from animals still serve that purpose in some places. Musicians discovered that striking a hollow metal bell makes a useful, strongly shaped sound.

Many musical cowbells have no clapper inside. The player holds the bell or fixes it on a stand, then strikes it with a stick. Different sizes and shapes give different voices. Where the stick lands matters too.

Cowbells are important in several Latin-music styles and also appear in rock and orchestral music. Tuned Alpine bells, sometimes called Almglocken, can supply particular notes. There is no single inventor of all these bells. Listen for the bell’s strong rhythm cutting through a much larger group.

PercussionOccasional guestAbout 1 min read aloud

Metallophone

A family of ringing metal bars

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion · An occasional orchestral guest.
  • How it sounds: Tuned metal bars struck with mallets; notes that can ring and overlap.
  • When it began: Metal-bar instruments have centuries-old histories in parts of Asia. Modern classroom designs developed during the twentieth century.
  • Players to know: Classroom ensembles and gamelan musicians; metallophone is a family name rather than one solo instrument.
  • A surprise: Glockenspiels and vibraphones are metallophones too: their sounding bars are metal.

The story

Metallophone means a musical instrument with tuned metal sounding bars. It names a family, rather than one exact design. A classroom metallophone often has a row of bars above a wooden box. A glockenspiel, vibraphone and several gamelan instruments are relatives in this broad family.

The player strikes a bar with a mallet. The metal vibrates and keeps ringing after the strike. Touching it gently can stop the note; musicians call that damping. Long ringing notes can overlap into a shimmering cloud.

Metal-bar instruments have been played for centuries in parts of Asia. Modern classroom versions belong to twentieth-century music education. There is no single inventor of the whole family. Compare a school metallophone with the slenthem in our gamelan section: related ideas can grow into very different instruments.

PercussionOccasional guestAbout 1 min read aloud

Thunder sheet

A storm inside a sheet of metal

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion · An occasional orchestral guest.
  • How it sounds: A large thin metal sheet is shaken, flexed or struck; rumbling, crashing noise.
  • When it began: Theatre makers used artificial thunder long before loudspeakers. Flexible metal thunder sheets became part of theatre and concert percussion.
  • Players to know: Played by theatre sound crews and orchestral percussionists rather than a usual soloist.
  • A surprise: The metal itself vibrates; there is no recording of real thunder hidden inside.

The story

A thunder sheet is a large, thin piece of metal that can wobble and bend. Shake or move it and the whole surface vibrates, making a deep, uneven rumble. A stronger movement can produce a startling crash.

Theatres needed storm sounds long before recorded sound and loudspeakers were available. They used several clever machines; a thunder sheet is one solution. It does not have one agreed inventor or birthday. Different sheets and playing methods give different kinds of storm.

Percussionists may shake, strike or rub the sheet when a score asks for a special sound. Unlike a glockenspiel, it is not normally there to play a neat scale. Listen with your eyes closed: can you picture distant thunder before the big crash arrives?

PercussionOccasional guestAbout 1 min read aloud

Wind machine

Turn a handle and hear a gale

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion · An occasional orchestral guest.
  • How it sounds: A rotating wooden drum rubs against fabric; a rising and falling rushing sound.
  • When it began: Mechanical wind effects grew through theatre traditions and entered orchestral scores by the late nineteenth century.
  • Players to know: Orchestral percussionists and theatre musicians; not usually a solo instrument.
  • A surprise: A traditional wind machine imitates wind by friction, rather than blowing a strong breeze at the audience.

The story

A musical wind machine can look like a wooden drum inside a frame. Turn its handle and the drum rubs against a strip of fabric. That friction makes a rushing sound, from a soft breeze to a noisy gale.

It belongs to the world of theatre sound effects as well as orchestral percussion. Mechanical storm effects existed before sound recordings. By the late nineteenth century, composers were inviting wind machines into concert scores too. Richard Strauss uses one in Don Quixote, helping us imagine an extraordinary adventure.

The player controls the speed and pressure so the weather fits the music. No great fan needs to blow across the audience! Listen to the sound grow and fade. Can the orchestra make you imagine wind without moving your hair?

PercussionOccasional guestAbout 2 min read aloud

Bongo drums

Two small drums have a quick conversation

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion · An occasional orchestral guest.
  • How it sounds: A joined pair of small hand drums; quick, bright taps and rounded tones.
  • When it began: Bongos developed in eastern Cuba around the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, drawing on African musical traditions.
  • Players to know: Mongo Santamaría, Armando Peraza and Giovanni Hidalgo.
  • A surprise: The two drums differ in size and pitch, giving one player two answering voices.

The story

Bongos come as a joined pair of small drums. A player may hold them between the knees or put them on a stand. Fingers and hands strike the stretched heads, producing quick taps, rolls and changing tones.

The smaller drum usually sounds higher than its partner. Pressing a head while playing can change its sound too. A skilled player does much more than alternate two notes: small changes of touch create a whole conversation.

Bongos developed in eastern Cuba around the turn of the twentieth century, drawing on African musical traditions. They became important in Cuban dance music and later in Latin jazz and other styles. Listen to Giovanni Hidalgo or another expert: can you follow the repeated pattern while the player adds little surprises around it?

A player can change the sound by using fingers, the palm or the edge of a hand, and by letting the skin ring or stopping it. Skilled hands combine these colours into repeating patterns. In a band, bongos fit with other percussion rather than simply making the same beat louder. Listen for a short answering phrase: can you hear the drummer leaving a space for the next musician?

PercussionOccasional guestAbout 2 min read aloud

Conga drums

Tall hand drums with many voices

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion · An occasional orchestral guest.
  • How it sounds: Hands strike a stretched head on a tall drum; deep tones, open rings and crisp slaps.
  • When it began: Congas developed in Afro-Cuban communities by the late nineteenth century, drawing particularly on Central African drum traditions.
  • Players to know: Chano Pozo, Mongo Santamaría, Cándido Camero, Carlos “Patato” Valdés and Giovanni Hidalgo.
  • A surprise: The Cuban name tumbadora is also used; players may arrange several sizes together.

The story

A conga is a tall drum with one stretched head. The player uses hands and fingers, finding a deep bass note, a ringing open tone or a sharp slap. Several drums of different sizes can sit together, giving one musician different voices to choose from.

Congas developed in Afro-Cuban communities, with important roots in Central African drumming. Wooden versions were in use by the late nineteenth century. In Cuba, tumbadora is another familiar name for the instrument.

The drums became central to rumba and travelled into Latin jazz, salsa and many other styles. Players such as Chano Pozo and Mongo Santamaría helped new audiences hear their possibilities. Watch a demonstration carefully: the fingers, palms and tiny changes of touch matter as much as the size of the drum.

The player can make open ringing tones, low sounds and sharp slaps by changing where and how the hands meet the skin. A repeating part may fit together with bells, claves and other drums, each adding something different. The pattern belongs to a musical conversation. Try following only one drum for a while, then listen to the whole group again. Can you hear how the parts interlock?

PercussionOccasional guestAbout 1 min read aloud

Bar chimes (mark tree)

A sweep of tiny metal sparkles

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Percussion · An occasional orchestral guest.
  • How it sounds: A row of hanging metal rods is brushed so the rods ring together.
  • When it began: The modern mark tree developed as a studio-percussion instrument in the late 1960s, associated with percussionist Mark Stevens.
  • Players to know: Studio, theatre and concert percussionists; Mark Stevens helped develop this instrument.
  • A surprise: A short sweep can suggest magic, a dream or a sudden change of scene.

The story

A row of little metal rods hangs from a wooden rail. Brush across them with a hand or beater and a sparkling shower of sound appears. These are bar chimes, also called a mark tree or chime tree.

The rods have different lengths. Rather than picking out a careful tune, a player usually sweeps across them for colour. Light, short touches and longer sweeps give different effects. The rods need room to swing and ring.

The modern mark tree developed in studio music in the late 1960s and is associated with percussionist Mark Stevens. Today it adds shimmer to recordings, theatre music and percussion groups. It is separate from tall tubular bells and from a single classroom chime bar. Close your eyes: what kind of scene could these tiny metal sparkles introduce?

Keyboards

Keys open the door to different sound worlds.

5 instruments
Contents ↑

These are grouped by how you play them. The piano has struck strings; the celesta has struck metal plates; the pipe organ uses air. They appear when a piece asks for them. Harp is listed with Strings.

KeyboardsMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Piano

A keyboard with little hammers inside

In a few notes

  • Section: Keyboards.
  • How it sounds: Keys make hammers strike strings; from gentle whispers to mighty chords.
  • When it began: Bartolomeo Cristofori developed the piano in Italy around 1700. The modern concert grand evolved through many later improvements.
  • Players to know: Clara Schumann, Martha Argerich, Lang Lang and Isata Kanneh-Mason.
  • A surprise: A modern concert piano usually has 88 keys. Its Italian name began as “soft-loud”.

The story

Press a piano key and a little hammer jumps towards a string. The hammer strikes, then springs away so the string can vibrate. A wooden soundboard helps the sound spread. Hidden inside a grand piano is a remarkable team of strings, hammers, levers and dampers.

A pianist can make notes louder or softer by changing the way the keys are played. That was an exciting feature of the early instrument. Its name grew from Italian words for “soft” and “loud”. Pedals add more choices: the right pedal lifts dampers so notes can keep ringing after the fingers leave the keys.

The Italian maker Bartolomeo Cristofori developed the piano around 1700. His instrument was smaller and lighter-sounding than a modern concert grand. Later makers added stronger frames, more keys and other improvements. Today’s large piano is the result of centuries of changing ideas and careful engineering.

The piano is a keyboard instrument, but its sound also links it to strings and percussion: hammers strike strings. It is not needed in every orchestral piece. In a concerto, it often takes the starring role, answering the orchestra or leading it into a new adventure. Listen for one hand carrying a tune while the other supplies a different pattern. Can you follow both, or do you prefer to choose one musical thread?

KeyboardsMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Celesta (celeste)

A secret box of bell-like sounds

In a few notes

  • Section: Keyboards.
  • How it sounds: Keys make felt hammers strike metal plates; delicate, bell-like notes.
  • When it began: The celesta was patented by the Mustel workshop in Paris in 1886, generally credited to Auguste Mustel.
  • Players to know: Orchestral keyboard players such as Philip Moore and Elizabeth Burley. Celesta parts are commonly played by pianists rather than separate solo specialists.
  • A surprise: Tchaikovsky used it for the Sugar Plum Fairy in The Nutcracker.

The story

A celesta looks like a small upright piano, but listen before deciding what it is. Its notes sound like little bells. The secret is inside: instead of striking strings, felt-covered hammers strike metal plates. Wooden resonating boxes below the plates help their delicate vibrations become easier to hear.

The player uses a keyboard, so pianists often play orchestral celesta parts. A pedal lets notes keep ringing. Although we have put it with keyboards so you can find it easily, the celesta also belongs to tuned percussion: its metal plates make the sound when struck. An instrument can be described in more than one useful way.

The celesta was patented in Paris in 1886 by the Mustel workshop and is generally credited to Auguste Mustel. Some historical accounts discuss the contributions of other members of the family. Unlike ancient drums or flutes, it belongs to a fairly recent chapter of instrument-making.

Tchaikovsky heard the instrument’s possibilities and used it in The Nutcracker. Its famous Sugar Plum Fairy music seems to tiptoe and sparkle. The celesta also appears in film music and other concert pieces. Listen for the gentle start of each note and the ring that follows. Could a loud, heavy instrument make the same dance feel completely different?

KeyboardsOccasional guestAbout 2 min read aloud

Pipe organ

A whole building full of breath

In a few notes

  • Section: Keyboards · An occasional orchestral guest.
  • How it sounds: Keys and pedals send air into pipes; many different voices, from whispers to thunder.
  • When it began: The ancient Greek hydraulis, associated with Ctesibius in the 200s BCE, is an early ancestor. Modern pipe organs developed over many centuries.
  • Players to know: Johann Sebastian Bach, Marie-Claire Alain, Gillian Weir and Anna Lapwood.
  • A surprise: An organist may play keyboards with the hands and a pedal keyboard with the feet.

The story

Some concert halls have an instrument so large that it seems part of the building. Rows of shining pipes stand above the stage. Behind them may be hundreds or thousands more. This is a pipe organ, an occasional orchestral guest with enough different voices to sound like a whole musical world.

The player presses keys to let air into selected pipes. Some pipes make sound when air meets an edge; others have vibrating reeds. Different sizes give different pitches. Stops let the organist choose groups of pipes and combine their colours. Several hand keyboards and a pedal keyboard make it possible to play with both hands and feet.

An ancient ancestor called the hydraulis was developed in the Greek world in the 200s BCE and is associated with Ctesibius. Its system used water to help regulate the air. Pipe organs changed enormously through the Middle Ages and later centuries. No single maker invented the complete modern organ.

An organ is not part of every orchestra and is often heard alone or with singers. But composers such as Saint-Saëns wrote orchestral music that uses its extraordinary power. Listen first for a quiet pipe colour, then a full grand chord. The difference is not simply loudness: many different sets of pipes can join the sound. Which voice would you choose for a lullaby, and which for a celebration?

Pipe organs became important in many Western Christian churches during the Middle Ages. They have accompanied singing, supported choirs and inspired music by organists such as J. S. Bach. Christian traditions differ: some churches use organs, others use different instruments or sing without instruments. Ancient Bible translations that use the word “organ” do not mean a modern pipe organ.

KeyboardsMeet the instrumentAbout 2 min read aloud

Harpsichord

A keyboard that plucks its own strings

In a few notes

  • Section: Keyboards.
  • How it sounds: Keys operate little plectrums that pluck strings; bright, crisp and ringing.
  • When it began: Harpsichords are documented in Europe by the late 1300s. Makers developed many regional designs during the 1500s–1700s.
  • Players to know: Wanda Landowska, Gustav Leonhardt, Trevor Pinnock and Jean Rondeau.
  • A surprise: Some harpsichords have two keyboards, called manuals, but they do not work like a piano’s loud and soft touch.

The story

At first glance, a harpsichord might look like a piano wearing an old-fashioned wooden coat. Look inside, though, and a different machine is at work. Press a key and a small upright piece called a jack rises. A tiny plectrum on the jack plucks a string, rather like a very small guitar pick.

Because the string is plucked, pressing harder does not make the same large change in loudness that it does on a piano. Players create expression through timing, the length of notes and the way musical lines fit together. Stops can bring different sets of strings into play. Some instruments also have two rows of keys.

Harpsichords were known in Europe by the late 1300s. Makers in Italy, Flanders, France and elsewhere developed their own designs. There was no single inventor of every kind. During the Baroque period, the harpsichord often helped provide the continuo: the musical foundation beneath singers or other instruments.

A harpsichordist might read a bass line with numbers showing which chords to add. That leaves room for careful musical choices, rather than simply copying every note from a page. The instrument also has wonderful solo music and concertos. Listen for its crisp plucks among smooth string sounds. Can a melody feel graceful and expressive even when the player cannot make each note louder by pressing harder?

KeyboardsOccasional guestAbout 2 min read aloud

Reed organ

A keyboard powered by air and tiny metal tongues

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Keyboards · An occasional orchestral guest.
  • How it sounds: Air makes metal free reeds vibrate; a steady, warm, reedy voice.
  • When it began: Reed keyboards developed around 1800; Alexandre Debain patented the harmonium in 1842. Many later designs followed.
  • Players to know: Jonathan Scott and Joris Verdin play historical harmoniums. Many church musicians played pump organs.
  • A surprise: A reed organ has no forest of sounding pipes: small vibrating reeds make the notes.

The story

A reed organ may look like a small piano, but opening it reveals a different sound machine. Air passes around thin metal tongues called free reeds. Pressing a key lets a selected reed speak. Foot pedals often pump the bellows that supply the air.

Several kinds developed around 1800. The name harmonium is especially linked with Alexandre Debain’s 1842 patent. Some instruments push air through reeds; others draw air in. Hand-pumped harmoniums also became important in South Asian music, where players developed distinctive techniques.

During the 1800s, reed organs helped lead singing in many smaller churches and chapels. They cost less and took less space than large pipe organs. Families also used them at home. Listen to a held chord: the notes can continue as long as the player supplies air. Can you hear the bellows helping the tune breathe?

Stops can bring extra sets of reeds into use, changing the colour or strength of the sound. On a foot-pumped instrument, the hands shape the tune while the feet keep the air moving. It takes practice to make that air supply feel smooth! A harmonium is therefore related to the accordion’s free reeds, even though its keyboard and furniture may remind you of a piano.

Handbells

A team that shares one shining melody

In a few notes

  • Section: Other · Percussion (tuned bells).
  • How it sounds: A clapper strikes inside a tuned metal bell; clear, ringing notes.
  • When it began: Hand-held bells have ancient roots. Tuned English handbell sets developed during the 1600s and 1700s, partly for practising tower-bell patterns.
  • Players to know: Ensembles such as the Raleigh Ringers and Sonos Handbell Ensemble; many church and community groups also perform.
  • A surprise: In a handbell team, one person may be responsible for only a few notes of a tune that everybody builds together.

The story

Imagine a melody divided between a whole team of people. Each person holds one or more handbells, waiting for the right moment to ring. One player begins a note, another answers, and the tune travels along the table. Music-making becomes a wonderfully visible act of teamwork.

A handbell has a metal bell, a handle and a clapper inside. The player moves the handle so the clapper strikes the bell. In a tuned set, different sizes give different notes. Bigger bells usually sound lower. Ringing clearly is only half the job: the player must also stop, or damp, a note at the right moment, often against the body or a padded surface.

Hand-held bells have been used in many cultures for a very long time. Tuned English handbell sets developed during the 1600s and 1700s, partly so tower-bell ringers could practise patterns without climbing into a bell tower. Over time, performers developed ways to play melodies, chords and specially written concert music.

Today, handbell ensembles play in churches, schools, community halls and concert venues. Some musicians ring several bells in each hand, and large sets can cover many octaves. Our listening examples include classical arrangements: those composers did not necessarily write the original music for handbells. Watch the players hand the tune along. How can everyone help a melody sound smooth when no one person plays every note?

English handbell ringing has close ties with church bell ringing: ringers could practise change-ringing patterns on smaller bells. Today handbell choirs perform in churches, schools and concert halls.

OtherBeyond the orchestraAbout 1 min read aloud

Washboard

Laundry equipment discovers a rhythm

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Other.
  • How it sounds: Scraping or tapping a ridged surface; brisk rattles, clicks and scratches.
  • When it began: Ribbed washboards were common household tools in the 1800s. They became familiar in American jug-band, blues and skiffle music during the 1900s.
  • Players to know: Washboard Sam, Washboard Chaz and Deryck Guyler.
  • A surprise: Some players wear sewing thimbles on their fingers to tap and scrape the ridges.

The story

A washboard once helped people clean clothes by rubbing wet cloth over its ridges. Musicians found another use: scrape or tap those ridges and a lively rhythm comes out. Some players wear thimbles on their fingers; others use small tools or brushes.

Household washboards were common during the 1800s. In the next century they became familiar in American jug bands, blues and later skiffle groups. Washboard Sam became a well-known blues performer with the instrument.

A musical washboard may carry extra bells, tins or small cymbals, making a little collection of sounds. The related zydeco rubboard is often worn on the chest, but it has its own history and shape. Listen for the scratchy rhythm underneath the singing: a useful household tool has turned into a musical companion.

Kalimba & thumb-piano relatives

Thumb pianos: kalimba, mbira and likembe relatives

In a few notes

  • Section: Around the World · Plucked idiophone (lamellophone).
  • How it sounds: Flexible metal tines plucked with the thumbs; gentle, bell-like notes.
  • When it began: African lamellophones have long histories. Hugh Tracey developed and marketed a particular modern kalimba design during the 1950s.
  • Players to know: Andrew Tracey, Mark Holdaway and Kevin Spears. Related mbira traditions include musicians such as Stella Chiweshe and Mbira DzeNharira.
  • A surprise: Its sound comes from metal tongues, not strings. The technical family name is lamellophone.

The story

A kalimba fits a row of musical notes into your hands. Metal strips called tines are fixed above a wooden board or hollow box. Press the end of a tine with a thumb and release it. The metal springs back and vibrates, making a clear, ringing note.

Longer tines usually sound lower than shorter ones. Many kalimbas put low notes near the middle, with higher notes alternating to the left and right. That means a scale may travel between your thumbs instead of moving steadily across a keyboard. Some instruments have a sound hole that can be partly covered to change the colour.

These instruments belong to the African lamellophone family: their sound comes from plucked flexible tongues. “Thumb piano” is a handy nickname, but they are not little string pianos. Names include kalimba, mbira, likembe and ikembe, depending on the community and instrument. These are related traditions, not interchangeable names for every design. Ikembe is used in Burundi and nearby regions; likembe names occur in Central Africa. Hugh Tracey developed a particular modern kalimba design during the 1950s.

Different lamellophones have their own tunings, techniques and cultural roles. Listen to a kalimba, then a likembe or mbira ensemble. Some sounds are smooth and bell-like; others have a lively buzz. Can you hear the repeating patterns meeting each other?

Ukulele

A small four-stringed traveller

In a few notes

  • Section: Around the World · Strings (plucked).
  • How it sounds: Usually four plucked or strummed strings; bright and friendly.
  • When it began: The ukulele developed in Hawaiʻi in the late 1800s from Portuguese instruments brought by immigrants, notably those who arrived from Madeira in 1879.
  • Players to know: Ernest Kaʻai, Israel Kamakawiwoʻole, Jake Shimabukuro and Taimane Gardner.
  • A surprise: Soprano, concert, tenor and baritone are common sizes. The baritone usually has a different tuning.

The story

A ukulele may look like a small guitar, but it has a story and a voice of its own. Most have four strings. A player can strum a chord with one finger or pluck separate notes to make a melody. The wooden body helps those small string vibrations become a bright musical sound.

Ukuleles come in several common sizes: soprano, concert, tenor and baritone. Smaller ones often sound brighter, while larger bodies can give more depth. Many soprano, concert and tenor instruments use a high G string, so the strings do not run from lowest to highest in the order you might expect. Baritones are usually tuned differently.

The ukulele developed in Hawaiʻi during the late 1800s. Portuguese immigrants brought related instruments, including small guitars, and a group arrived from Madeira in 1879. Makers and Hawaiian musicians helped create a new local tradition. The instrument became part of Hawaiian musical life before travelling widely around the world.

The ukulele is not a standard member of a symphony orchestra. Here it belongs to our extra instruments to explore. Players use it for songs, instrumental solos and arrangements, including classical melodies originally written for other instruments. Listen to one performance with strummed chords and another with fingerpicked notes. How many musical jobs can just four strings manage at once?

Hammered dulcimer

A whole table of strings, played with tiny hammers

In a few notes

  • Section: Around the World · Strings (struck zither).
  • How it sounds: Strings stretched over a wooden box, struck with light beaters; ringing and sparkling.
  • When it began: Struck zithers have centuries of history across Europe and Asia. Hammered dulcimers are documented in medieval Europe; related instruments include the Persian santur and Chinese yangqin.
  • Players to know: Malcolm Dalglish, Dan Landrum and Maggie Sansone. The cimbalom is a larger concert relative, played by musicians such as Aladár Rácz.
  • A surprise: The Appalachian mountain dulcimer is a different instrument: it has frets and is usually plucked or strummed.

The story

The hammered dulcimer looks like a small wooden table crossed by rows of strings. Its player holds a light beater in each hand and taps the strings. Each stroke starts a bright vibration, and the wooden soundboard helps it travel into the room. A quick melody can seem to sparkle across the instrument.

Many notes use more than one string tuned together. Bridges divide the strings into useful vibrating lengths. The player must learn where the notes are and aim carefully, rather like a marimba player finding the right bars. Some instruments have ways to damp the ringing sound; others let the notes overlap more freely.

Hammered dulcimers belong to a large world of struck-string instruments with centuries of history in Europe and Asia. They were known in medieval Europe, while related traditions include the Persian santur and Chinese yangqin. Their development was not the work of one inventor. The larger concert cimbalom later gained pedals and a place in some orchestral scores.

There is a naming trap! The Appalachian mountain dulcimer is a different, fretted instrument, usually played by plucking or strumming. Here we are listening to the hammered kind. It appears in folk music, new compositions and arrangements of classical tunes. Watch the beaters bounce away after each strike: why would holding a beater against a string stop it from ringing?

Erhu

Two strings, a bow and a wonderfully human voice

In a few notes

  • Section: Around the World · Strings (bowed).
  • How it sounds: Two bowed strings and a small resonating body; expressive, sliding and singing.
  • When it began: The erhu belongs to the Chinese huqin family, with roots around a thousand years old. Its modern solo tradition developed strongly in the early 1900s.
  • Players to know: Liu Tianhua, Hua Yanjun (Abing), Min Huifen and Song Fei.
  • A surprise: The bow hair passes between the two strings, rather than being lifted completely away from them during ordinary playing.

The story

An erhu has a long narrow neck rising from a small sound box. Only two strings stretch along it. The player sits with the instrument upright and moves a bow sideways. Its voice can sound astonishingly close to someone singing, with gentle slides, shivers and changes of feeling.

The bow hair runs between the two strings. By controlling its contact, the player chooses which string speaks. Fingers press the strings without a violin-style fingerboard underneath. That allows smooth changes of pitch, but it also asks for a very accurate ear. The small resonating body helps turn the strings’ vibrations into a strong musical voice.

The erhu belongs to the Chinese huqin family of bowed instruments, whose roots reach back around a thousand years. Its present design and musical role developed over a long time. In the early 1900s, musicians including Liu Tianhua helped build a rich tradition of solo pieces and teaching methods.

The erhu is important in Chinese ensembles and orchestras, as well as solo performances. It is not a standard member of the Western symphony orchestra, though composers sometimes bring those sound worlds together. Listen to a slow phrase, then a lively one. Can two strings suggest both a thoughtful person speaking and a bird darting quickly through the air? A small number of strings does not mean a small number of musical possibilities.

Sitar

Plucked strings with a halo of answering notes

In a few notes

  • Section: Around the World · Strings (plucked lute).
  • How it sounds: Plucked strings over movable frets, with extra sympathetic strings; bright, buzzing and resonant.
  • When it began: The sitar developed in the Indian subcontinent, reaching recognisable forms during the 1700s and changing further in the 1800s and 1900s.
  • Players to know: Ravi Shankar, Vilayat Khan, Nikhil Banerjee and Anoushka Shankar.
  • A surprise: Sympathetic strings can vibrate along with played notes even when the musician does not pluck them directly.

The story

A sitar has a long neck, curved movable frets and a rounded resonating body, often made from a gourd. Its sound begins when a musician plucks a string with a small wire plectrum called a mizrab. The bridge helps give the note its distinctive bright, buzzing colour.

There are more strings than the player usually uses for the main melody. Some provide drones or rhythmic sounds. Others run underneath and vibrate sympathetically when matching notes are played. They add a shimmering halo around the tune. The player can also pull a string sideways across a fret, bending its pitch into long expressive curves.

The sitar developed in the Indian subcontinent, with recognisable forms appearing during the 1700s. Makers and musicians changed it further in later centuries. Its story cannot reliably be reduced to one inventor. Different playing traditions favour different designs, numbers of strings and ways of shaping a musical phrase.

The sitar is especially associated with Hindustani classical music from northern India. A raga offers a framework of notes and musical ideas, while a tala organises repeating rhythmic cycles. This is a classical tradition with its own history, not simply an unusual addition to European music. Sitarists also play concertos and other collaborations with orchestras. Listen for the main melody and the answering resonance beneath it. How many layers can you notice in just one plucked note?

Gamelan

A whole musical team, not just one instrument

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Around the World.
  • How it sounds: An ensemble of gongs, metal-bar instruments and drums, sometimes joined by voices, strings and flutes.
  • When it began: Indonesian gamelan traditions are centuries old. Earlier musical groups appear in temple carvings from the 700s; there was no single inventor.
  • Players to know: Community ensembles across Indonesia; master artists include Ki Purbo Asmoro and Ki Blacius Subono.
  • A surprise: A gamelan is also the name for its specially matched set of instruments.

The story

Gamelan is a team of instruments and musicians from Indonesia. It is not the name of one enormous instrument! Gongs, rows of metal bars and drums often form its heart. Voices, bamboo flutes and string instruments may join them.

Different parts fit together like a musical puzzle. One player may carry a steady melody while others add quicker patterns. A deep gong can mark a meeting point. Java and Bali have different gamelan traditions, and each set has its own tuning.

In Central Java, musicians use tuning systems called sléndro and pélog. They do not divide up the notes in exactly the same way as a piano. Even two gamelans using the same system can have different tunings. Their instruments are made to belong together, rather like members of one musical family.

These traditions grew over centuries, rather than beginning with one inventor. Carvings at the Borobudur temple show earlier musical groups in the 700s. Today children and adults learn from experienced musicians. Gamelan accompanies concerts, ceremonies, dancing and theatre. Listen for the teamwork: can you follow one repeating pattern while another moves around it?

A gamelan can also help tell a story in a shadow-puppet performance. Try listening twice: first follow the lowest gong, then choose a higher, busier sound. Did you notice something new the second time?

Axatse

A gourd wearing a rattling coat

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Around the World.
  • How it sounds: Beads or seeds on an outside net strike a dried gourd.
  • When it began: A traditional West African rattle, especially associated with Ewe communities in Ghana and Togo. Its first maker and date are unknown.
  • Players to know: Ewe and Akan community musicians; it is commonly heard as part of an ensemble rather than a solo-star instrument.
  • A surprise: Unlike a maraca, its rattling pieces sit outside the hollow shell.

The story

An axatse is a dried gourd with a net of rattling beads or seeds around its round body. The player holds its neck and moves it so that the net knocks against the shell. In Ewe music, it may alternate between the other hand and the thigh.

This percussion instrument helps hold a group together. Its repeating pattern fits with bells and drums, while singers and dancers join the music. Ewe communities in Ghana and Togo are especially associated with it. Related rattles have other names among neighbouring peoples.

Nobody can point to its first maker or a certain invention date. The skill has been passed between generations. Watch the player’s hands, then close your eyes: can you still hear exactly where the repeating pattern begins?

Calung

Bamboo tubes that play a tune

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Around the World.
  • How it sounds: Tuned bamboo tubes struck with beaters; woody, hollow and lively.
  • When it began: Calung belongs to long-established musical traditions of Java, Indonesia. A Sundanese example in The Met dates from the late 1800s; its original invention date is unknown.
  • Players to know: Sundanese and Banyumasan community ensembles in Java.
  • A surprise: Bamboo is a grass, even though its strong hollow stems can look like wooden poles.

The story

The calung makes music from bamboo. Its tubes are cut and tuned so that striking different ones produces different notes. Imagine a row of hollow plants becoming a musical voice!

Calung traditions belong to Java in Indonesia, including Sundanese music in the west and Banyumasan music farther east. The name can describe related instruments or a musical group. Some tubes hang in a row; other forms use a frame that the musician can hold. Players strike the bamboo rather than shaking it like an angklung.

There is no certain date for the first calung. Museums preserve examples from the late 1800s, showing that this is an established tradition. Listen to the clear, hollow notes. Can a group make several little patterns join into one lively tune?

Caxixi

A tiny basket with a busy voice

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Around the World.
  • How it sounds: Seeds shake against woven sides and a hard gourd base.
  • When it began: A Brazilian basket rattle, especially known in Afro-Brazilian capoeira music. Its exact origins and invention date are uncertain.
  • Players to know: Capoeira musicians and Brazilian percussionists; it often accompanies a berimbau player.
  • A surprise: The same hand can hold a caxixi and the stick that strikes a berimbau.

The story

A caxixi looks like a small woven basket with a handle. Hidden inside are seeds or other little rattling pieces. Its bottom is often a flat piece of dried gourd. Shake the basket and the pieces knock against its sides or base.

This percussion instrument is closely linked with Brazil. In capoeira, a tradition combining movement, music and martial art, a musician may hold it while playing the berimbau musical bow. One movement can produce both the bow’s note and the basket’s rattle.

Its beginnings are uncertain, so there is no reliable single birthday to give it. Today caxixis also appear in percussion groups and popular music. Listen carefully to a small shake: even a tiny instrument can add a very important layer to a big musical pattern.

Didgeridoo

A low drone shaped by breath and mouth

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Around the World.
  • How it sounds: Vibrating lips set air moving inside a long tube; a deep drone with changing colours.
  • When it began: Developed by Aboriginal peoples of northern Australia before European colonisation. Its exact age is uncertain, and regional traditions have their own names.
  • Players to know: Djalu Gurruwiwi, a renowned Yolŋu yidaki musician and teacher.
  • A surprise: Yidaki is a Yolŋu name; it is not the name used by every Aboriginal language group.

The story

A didgeridoo is a long tube played by gently vibrating the lips. It makes a low drone, but that is only the beginning. Changing the tongue, cheeks and voice reshapes the sound into lively pulses and surprising colours.

The instrument comes from Aboriginal peoples of northern Australia. Different language groups have their own names and traditions; yidaki belongs to Yolŋu culture. Its exact age is uncertain. Makers have used bamboo and eucalyptus, including wood naturally hollowed by termites.

Skilled musicians can use circular breathing: the cheeks keep air moving briefly while the nose takes another breath. The music often accompanies singing and clapsticks.

The player’s mouth is part of the sound-making system. Try saying “ee” and then “oo” quietly: your tongue and lips move, changing the shape of the air space. A didgeridoo musician uses careful changes inside the mouth to colour the drone. Adding the voice can produce another layer, so one person may seem to make several sounds together.

This music belongs to living communities, with knowledge passed on by experienced musicians. Djalu Gurruwiwi was a renowned Yolŋu yidaki player and teacher. Listen to a traditional player as well as a demonstration. Can you hear how many different sounds grow from a tube with no finger holes?

Bougarabou

Several drums, one pair of clever hands

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Around the World.
  • How it sounds: Hands strike a skin stretched over a tall wooden drum; deep tones and sharper taps.
  • When it began: A Jola (Diola) drumming tradition from Senegal and neighbouring parts of The Gambia and Guinea-Bissau. No certain invention date is known.
  • Players to know: Saikouba Badjie, a master Jola drummer recorded playing this tradition.
  • A surprise: A single drummer can play a group of differently tuned bougarabou drums.

The story

A bougarabou is a tall wooden drum with a stretched skin head. Its rounded low notes can be followed by crisp taps from the player’s fingers. Sometimes one musician sits among several drums and moves between them, making a whole conversation of rhythms.

This is a Jola, or Diola, musical tradition from Senegal and nearby parts of The Gambia and Guinea-Bissau. It accompanies community dancing and important occasions. People may sing and clap alongside the drummer, so the music belongs to the whole gathering.

The tradition developed over generations; no certain first design date is known. Saikouba Badjie is a renowned recorded performer. Watch how the hands travel between drums. Can you tap one steady beat while the drummer fits many changing patterns around it?

Bagpipes

A bag of air keeps the music flowing

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Around the World.
  • How it sounds: A squeezed air bag feeds reeds in melody pipes and, often, steady drone pipes.
  • When it began: Bagpipes were described in the ancient Mediterranean world and spread widely in medieval Europe. Scottish pipes are one branch of a much larger family.
  • Players to know: Kathryn Tickell plays Northumbrian pipes; many other piping traditions have their own great musicians.
  • A surprise: Some bagpipes use elbow-powered bellows instead of a blowing tube.

The story

Bagpipes carry their own little store of air. The player fills a bag, then squeezes it to send air through pipes with vibrating reeds. Fingers choose notes on a melody pipe called a chanter. Other pipes often hold steady notes called drones.

Scottish Highland pipes are famous, but they are only one branch of a worldwide family. Bagpipes are played in Ireland, Spain, France, North Africa and many other places. Some are powerful outdoor instruments; others have gentle indoor voices. Air may come from the mouth or from small bellows under an elbow.

Bagpipes were described in ancient Mediterranean times and became widespread in medieval Europe. No single person invented all their forms. A bag lets the tune continue while a mouth-blown piper takes a breath. But keeping the air steady still takes skill. The fingers often add quick little notes to shape the melody. Listen for those tiny musical decorations: they can make a repeated note seem to bounce.

Northumbrian smallpipes have a closed-ended chanter, and many sets have keys that provide extra notes. Their quieter, separated notes offer a different sound from the flowing voice of Highland pipes. The instrument’s whole design helps shape the music people play.

Listen to Kathryn Tickell’s Northumbrian pipes, then compare Highland pipes. Which sound would suit a quiet room, and which a parade?

Slenthem

A low, glowing voice in the gamelan

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Around the World.
  • How it sounds: Metal bars hang above resonating tubes and are struck with a padded beater.
  • When it began: A Javanese gamelan instrument, probably developed in the later 1800s from related metal-bar designs.
  • Players to know: Javanese gamelan musicians; it is an ensemble role rather than a usual solo-star instrument.
  • A surprise: Its name is also written slentem; it is related to the gendèr family.

The story

The slenthem is a low-pitched metal-bar instrument from Java, Indonesia. It belongs inside a gamelan ensemble. A musician strikes its suspended bars with a padded beater, making mellow notes that help carry the main outline of the tune.

Below each bar is a tube that strengthens its sound. The player also touches bars to stop notes ringing for too long. This is called damping. Choosing when a sound ends can be just as important as choosing when it starts!

The modern slenthem probably developed in the later 1800s from earlier gamelan designs. Its notes belong to its own ensemble’s tuning, rather than simply copying the white keys of a piano. Listen for this calm, low layer beneath the busier sounds. Can you follow its melody through the musical crowd?

Cajón

A wooden box becomes a drum

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Around the World.
  • How it sounds: Hands strike a thin wooden face; deep knocks and sharp taps.
  • When it began: The Afro-Peruvian cajón developed during the 1800s. Other Latin American box-drum traditions have their own histories.
  • Players to know: Caitro Soto, Susana Baca’s ensembles and many Afro-Peruvian musicians.
  • A surprise: Cajón is a Spanish word for a large box or drawer.

The story

A cajón is an instrument you can sit on! The player sits on top of a sturdy wooden box and reaches down to strike its front face. Tapping near the edge gives a different colour from striking nearer the middle. A hole lets sound out of the hollow body.

The cajón has an especially important place in Afro-Peruvian music. Its familiar form developed during the 1800s, using the musical possibilities of wooden boxes. Other Latin American communities have their own box-drum traditions too.

Some modern cajóns contain strings or metal snares for a buzzing sound; traditional Peruvian versions need not have these. The instrument later became popular in flamenco and many other styles. Listen to the deep and sharp strokes working together like a tiny drum kit.

A player can use fingertips, the flat hand and different striking places to shape a whole vocabulary of sounds. The box itself acts as a resonator, strengthening the moving wooden face. Musicians learn patterns from particular traditions rather than treating every rhythm as the same. In a group, the cajón may answer a singer or support dancers. Try listening to its deep strokes separately from its sharp taps.

Clapsticks

Two pieces of wood keep a living rhythm

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Around the World.
  • How it sounds: Two shaped wooden sticks strike together; clear, carrying clicks.
  • When it began: Clapsticks belong to longstanding Aboriginal Australian musical traditions. Names and designs vary between communities; there is no single invention date.
  • Players to know: Aboriginal singers and community musicians; particular names and uses belong to particular communities.
  • A surprise: Bilma and bimla are among regional names; no one name covers every Aboriginal language.

The story

Clapsticks make music when two pieces of shaped hardwood meet. The sound can be sharp and clear, helping singers and dancers share a pulse. Shape, timber and the place of contact all affect the click.

These instruments belong to longstanding Aboriginal Australian musical traditions. Different communities have their own names, playing styles and cultural meanings. Bilma and bimla are among the names used in some regions. It would be misleading to give all clapsticks one inventor or birthday.

Clapsticks may accompany singing, dancing and, in some northern traditions, didgeridoo. They are more than classroom rhythm sticks: the music belongs to living communities. Listen to a public performance and notice how the wooden pulse supports the voice. Does it stay steady while the singer’s phrases change?

Bugle

A clear call before the valves arrived

In a few notes

  • Section: Historical & early music · Brass.
  • How it sounds: Buzzing lips and an open tube, usually without valves; clear signalling calls.
  • When it began: The familiar military bugle developed during the late 1700s from earlier signalling horns. Keyed and valved relatives appeared in the 1800s.
  • Players to know: Oliver Willcox Norton, associated with the early performance of Taps, and ceremonial bugler Keith Clark.
  • A surprise: An ordinary valveless bugle uses a natural series of notes rather than all the notes a modern trumpet can play.

The story

Before radios and loudspeakers, a clear musical call could carry a message across a large outdoor space. A bugle might signal that it was time to wake up, gather together or remember someone. Its bright voice made a short pattern easier to recognise than a person shouting from far away.

An ordinary bugle is a brass tube with a mouthpiece and a flared bell, usually without valves or a slide. The player buzzes the lips and changes breath and lip control to choose notes from the instrument’s natural harmonic series. It cannot simply play every note of an ordinary scale. Composers and callers work creatively within that smaller set.

The familiar military bugle developed during the late 1700s from earlier signalling horns. During the 1800s, makers added keys or valves to some related instruments. Those changes helped create new possibilities, but they also made instruments with different jobs and names. A cornet is not just an ordinary bugle with a new label.

We have placed the bugle in our historical section because of its important signalling story, but it is still used today. Ceremonial calls such as the Last Post and Taps remain familiar. A call is not always a concert piece, yet careful rhythm, breath and tone still matter. Listen to the space after the last note: what can a very short melody make people feel?

In Australia, the ceremony call you may be thinking of is the Last Post. It is sounded at military funerals and remembrance ceremonies, including Anzac Day, to honour those who died in service. The Australian War Memorial also holds a daily Last Post Ceremony. Its ceremonial purpose differs from a concert solo.

Viol (viola da gamba)

A bowed string family with frets

In a few notes

  • Section: Historical & early music · Strings (bowed viol family).
  • How it sounds: Bowed strings over a fretted fingerboard; clear, warm and intimate.
  • When it began: Viols developed in Europe around the late 1400s and early 1500s and flourished during the Renaissance and Baroque periods.
  • Players to know: Marin Marais, Sainte-Colombe, Jordi Savall, Hille Perl and Paolo Pandolfo.
  • A surprise: Viola da gamba means “viol of the leg”: even smaller viols are held upright, rather than under the chin.

The story

A viol can look a little like a cello at first, but it belongs to a different string family. Look for the frets tied around its neck, rather like a guitar’s note markers. Many viols have six strings, though other numbers exist. Their shape and tuning differ from instruments of the violin family.

The name viola da gamba means “viol of the leg”. Players hold the instrument upright, supported between or against the legs. They usually hold the bow from underneath. Their fingers can adjust the bow hair’s tension while playing. Those details help shape a wonderfully flexible and intimate sound.

Viols developed in Europe around the late 1400s and early 1500s. They became important in Renaissance and Baroque music. There were treble, tenor and bass sizes, as well as other variants. Groups of viols could play together in a consort, with separate musical lines weaving like voices in a choir.

The bass viol also became a solo instrument. In France, players and composers such as Sainte-Colombe and Marin Marais explored its rich possibilities. Viols later became less common, but modern musicians brought renewed interest to their music. Historical does not mean silent or forgotten! Listen to a bass viol alone, then to a consort. Can you recognise a shared family colour even when the instruments speak at different heights?

Lyre

Strings held between two arms

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Historical & early music.
  • How it sounds: Strings are plucked with fingers or a pick; clear and ringing.
  • When it began: Lyres existed in Mesopotamia by the third millennium BCE, more than 4,000 years ago. Different cultures developed different forms.
  • Players to know: Michael Levy and Peter Pringle explore reconstructed ancient lyres. Living lyre traditions also have their own expert players.
  • A surprise: A lyre has strings stretched from a soundbox to a crossbar between two arms.

The story

Imagine a little frame with strings stretched across its open middle. At the bottom sits a soundbox; two arms hold a crossbar above it. This is the basic lyre shape. A player plucks the strings and may stop unwanted strings from ringing with the other hand.

Lyres were played in ancient Mesopotamia, Egypt and Greece, with many different shapes and string arrangements. Archaeologists have found famous lyres at Ur dating from the third millennium BCE. Modern reconstructions help us explore possible sounds, but we cannot recover every detail of an ancient performance.

In 1 Samuel 16, David plays a kinnor for Saul. This ancient instrument is commonly understood as a lyre, though some Bible translations say harp. It was not a modern orchestral harp. Listen for the separate plucks joining into a tune.

The strings do not lie over a long fingerboard like a violin’s. On many lyres, each open string supplies a note, and the musician chooses which strings to let ring. Lyres are still played in parts of Africa as well as in ancient-music reconstructions. They are a whole family: a Greek lyre and an Ethiopian krar share a broad idea but have different designs and musical traditions.

Sackbut

Meet the early trombone

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Historical & early music.
  • How it sounds: Buzzing lips and a moving slide; rounded, flexible and singing.
  • When it began: The double-slide trombone developed in Europe during the 1400s. Sackbut is a historical English name.
  • Players to know: Adam Woolf, Sue Addison and members of the English Cornett & Sackbut Ensemble.
  • A surprise: Many sackbuts have smaller bells than modern trombones, helping them blend with voices.

The story

A sackbut is an early kind of trombone. Its player buzzes into a mouthpiece and moves a double slide. Pulling the slide out lengthens the air tube, making lower notes possible. The instrument developed in Europe during the 1400s.

Compared with many modern trombones, historical sackbuts often have a narrower tube and a smaller, less flared bell. Their voices can blend beautifully with singers. Makers built different sizes, so a group could cover higher and lower musical parts.

Sackbuts played at courts, civic celebrations and church services. In Renaissance and early Baroque church music they could support choir parts or join other instruments. Modern early-music groups use surviving instruments and careful copies to explore those sounds. Listen to a choir with sackbuts: can you tell when a human voice and a brass voice are moving together?

The slide gives a player many possible tube lengths, but it does not choose the correct note by itself. Listening carefully and controlling the lips are essential. Musicians usually aim for clean steps between notes, rather than sliding everywhere. A group of sackbuts can play an independent piece, accompany singers, or answer a brighter cornett ensemble. Try following the lowest part as it supports the other voices.

You may spot the word “sackbut” in an old English Bible translation of Daniel 3. That is a translator’s historical instrument word; it does not mean that this Renaissance slide instrument existed in Daniel’s time.

Serpent

A wooden snake with a brass-family voice

Photograph to follow.

In a few notes

  • Section: Historical & early music.
  • How it sounds: Buzzing lips, a curved wooden tube and finger holes; a low, breathy bass voice.
  • When it began: The serpent appeared in France around the late 1500s. Its precise invention story is uncertain.
  • Players to know: Michel Godard, Douglas Yeo and Patrick Wibart.
  • A surprise: It belongs with lip-buzzed brass instruments even though its body is usually wood covered in leather.

The story

This instrument looks like a snake standing on its tail. Its wooden tube curves back and forth so that finger holes stay within reach. The player buzzes into a cup-shaped mouthpiece, much as a brass player does. That makes the serpent a brass-family wind instrument despite its wooden body.

Serpents appeared in France around the late 1500s. They became especially useful for supporting the low notes of church choirs. Later, changed designs joined military bands. Their low voice helped fill a space that other bass wind instruments would eventually occupy.

There are no valves on a traditional church serpent. Fingers cover holes while breath and lips help guide the notes. Today musicians use serpents in historical performances and new music, including jazz. Listen for a voice that can seem both grand and slightly rough around the edges.

To make the sound steady and in tune, a player must listen closely while adjusting breath, lips and fingerings. Covering a hole changes the vibrating air inside, but the instrument does not behave exactly like a recorder. Its bent body makes a long bass tube manageable. In a choir, that low voice could help singers follow their line before modern tubas and many other bass instruments existed.

A few musical words

Pitch: how high or low a note sounds. Tone colour: the special character of a sound. Melody: a tune. Concerto: a piece where a soloist or small group plays with a larger ensemble. Octave: the distance between a note and the next higher or lower note with the same letter name. Reed: a thin piece of material that vibrates when you blow. Glissando: a slide or sweep between notes.

The orchestra has no single unchanging instrument list. This guide covers common symphonic instruments, some guests, historical instruments and sound worlds from many cultures. Bible notes identify ancient instruments or close relatives, not identical modern designs. Ancient instrument words can be uncertain, and Bible translations differ. A historical connection does not mean that every Christian tradition has used the same instruments. Many more percussion instruments and special variants exist. Keyboards are grouped for easy browsing, even where their sound-making method also belongs to strings or percussion.
